## Index (50)

- **architecture-overview**: nexus-flow is an agent-native, offline-first suite — the board, the memory and the channel your agents work from — and nothing else.
- **priority-storage-canonical-ordinal**: Priority is a plugin-named label at the SURFACE but stored as the canonical ORDINAL — never store the label, or --json stops being plugin-independent.
- **op-struct-external-constructors**: crates/sync constructs core Op {} literals, so changing the Op struct is not confined to crates/core — grep the whole workspace before touching it.
- **nexflowit-plugin-is-proprietary**: The nexflow.it plugin is proprietary and must never live in this repo — the registry lets a consumer link its own without an OSS edit.
- **relay-ships-sqlite-and-postgres-not-dynamodb**: The shipped nxf-relay carries SQLite + Postgres, NOT DynamoDB — and rustls stays pinned to default-features=false + ring, the provider named.
- **the-running-binary-decides-the-service-instance**: An installed nxs is ALWAYS the production instance; only a build reads NXS_SERVICE_INSTANCE, and it says which, not whether.
- **branching**: Always work on a feat/-style branch — NEVER commit to main directly unless the user has explicitly allowed it for that piece of work.
- **build-test**: What CI actually runs, and what the local loop cannot see: the guide-topic map, the stale-binary symlink trap, and pruning target/ by SIZE.
- **conventions-patterns**: TDD for all behavior, --json everywhere, and every new CLI verb needs a counterpart on the library seam — a gate enforces that parity.
- **changelog-scope**: A changelog fragment is required by PRODUCT IMPACT, not by 'touches the CLI' — and none is written for a fix to something that never shipped publicly.
- **no-concurrent-lean-build-during-tests**: Never run the lean build while tests run — it overwrites target/debug/nxs and the MCP tests fail as if the code were broken.
- **det-ids-env-test-race**: NXF_DETERMINISTIC_IDS is process-global — never toggle it in a test that asserts id order; capture the ids and assert against sorted(captured).
- **engine-seam-test-rule**: A new public Engine::* seam is not done without a test AT THAT SEAM — CLI or facade coverage does not count, because the products speak Engine::*.
- **nxc-sidecar-ships-with-the-binary**: The nxc sidecar is COMPILED INTO the nxs binary since v0.54.0 — the side-by-side route had a bootstrap hole no version could close.
- **never-review-your-own-work-order**: The implementing agent NEVER starts the review — not for safety, not when the gates are green; the owner or PM starts it in a fresh session.
- **sync-postgres-driver-needs-off-runtime**: The sync postgres driver owns its own runtime: inside async it panics, in a Drop it aborts — wrap every entry point, the Drop included.
- **handover-lists-are-themselves-unverified**: A list handed over at closing time is itself unverified — derive it AGAIN from the vocabulary of the gap instead of working through it.
- **gate-evidence-is-per-commit**: A gate result proves EXACTLY the tree it ran against — HEAD plus the working copy; a run that raced anything proves nothing, green or red.
- **sweep-the-deleted-vocabulary**: After a removal you cannot grep for what is gone — search the vocabulary of what was DELETED, and compare against the branch base, not HEAD.
- **a-test-name-is-a-claim**: A test's NAME is a claim that can be false while all stays green — only mutation finds it, and a mutation that reds nothing is itself a finding.
- **a-relayed-claim-becomes-yours**: If you hand out work and pass on the reports, you become the author of every claim you let through — a claim you cannot re-run is not evidence.
- **the-board-is-local-and-not-in-git**: The board is git-ignored, single-device and lives outside the tree (.nxs is a symlink) — and there is no task type, only the plugin set.
- **handover-notes-are-not-durable-memory**: Where a session stopped belongs in the session-handover skill, never in durable memory.
- **shell-evaluates-long-descriptions**: Never pass a long description in double quotes — the shell evaluates backticks and angle brackets first; use a quoted heredoc and read it back.
- **gates-run-in-ci-not-locally**: NEVER run cargo clippy locally — only the test file you changed, plus cargo fmt; CI is the gate, and this goes in EVERY subagent prompt.
- **review-session-in-a-shared-checkout-mistakes-the-work-for-its-own**: A review session in a shared checkout can mistake foreign commits for its own work and refuse — say so up front, and forbid cargo there.
- **the-project-language-is-english**: Write everything down in English — tickets, memories, commits, PRs, code, docs; speak to a human in their language, but never write it down.
- **a-tickets-own-measurement-is-unverified**: A measurement pasted into a ticket is the TICKET'S evidence, not yours — re-run it before any removal, and hold when it comes out otherwise.
- **nxm-remember-has-no-stdin-dash**: nxm remember has no - STDIN form: piping a body stores a literal hyphen and reports success — pass it as an argument and verify with recall.
- **aws-account-ids-never-in-the-repo**: Never put an AWS account id in code, a PR or the git log — it comes from a GitHub secret at runtime, and tests use the example id 123456789012.
- **declared-members-bare-caller-qualified**: Channel members are recorded BARE while a caller arrives QUALIFIED — compare through facade::same_identity, never == or a SQL handle join.
- **flock-ends-at-the-last-close-not-the-holders**: An flock ends at the LAST close of its open file description — any fork keeps it alive, so always LOCK_UN in an explicit Drop.
- **claude-agent-sdk-scoping-airgap**: To air-gap a claude-agent-sdk subagent set setting_sources=[], strict_mcp_config=True and mcp_servers={} — else it inherits your MCP and the web.
- **parallel-worktree-agents-race**: Never launch two worktree-isolated agents in ONE message — a subagent checkout -b can flip the shared checkout; stagger and forbid checkout.
- **golden-harness-runs-in-crate-dir**: The trycmd golden harness runs in crates/cli with a pinned $HOME — a command that persists state outside the workspace cannot be a golden case.
- **facade-watch-test-flaky**: A full cargo test --all occasionally reds on a facade delete-and-recreate test — that is a CLASS, not one test; isolate, repeat, then judge.
- **slow-tests-check-target-deps-and-swap**: 88-122 min for cargo test --all is NORMAL here (external HFS+ disk) — only a sudden drop below that baseline is worth diagnosing.
- **launchd-install-is-not-home-isolated**: A pinned $HOME does NOT isolate launchd — RealCtl refuses outside the real login session, and still no test runs the real install.
- **nxs-init-writes-the-real-registry**: nxs init writes to the real background-service registry (~/.nexusflow/workspaces.toml) on every run — any black-box test that runs it MUST pin $HOME.
- **linux-process-start-is-reconstructed**: On Linux a process start time is RECONSTRUCTED from boot time plus ticks and can be a second off — never assert it against a wall clock.
- **cfg-split-kills-the-callee-elsewhere**: Splitting a function with #[cfg(target_os)] can make its callee dead code on the OTHER platform — use a cfg!() constant when you are only branching.
- **ci-cache-and-runtime-noise**: A single CI runtime here is noise (259-744 s on full cache hits) — never tune save-if; the cache sweeper deletes on ABSENCE in its branch arm.
- **call-graph-gate-joins-on-bare-names**: The chat write-seam gate joins calls by BARE NAME — a private helper called resolve or send turns eleven read verbs red; name helpers specifically.
- **golden-json-determinism-and-fixed-ids**: nxf JSON determinism needs serde_json WITHOUT preserve_order — xtask must never enable it, or feature unification breaks the goldens.
- **macos-ci-jobs-are-two-different-machines**: macOS tests (hosted) is a GitHub 3-core runner, not the org Mac — a hosted red is often a race, and a green check list can hide a cancelled run.
- **macos-libressl-no-ed25519-blake2b**: macOS system openssl is LibreSSL: no blake2b512, no Ed25519 — minisign-via-openssl cannot cover stock macOS; nxs self-update is the backstop.
- **oidc-no-repository-owner-condition**: A GitHub OIDC role trust in the nxsflow accounts must NOT carry a repository_owner condition — it breaks AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.
- **changelog-check-needs-a-commit**: changelog check reads a three-dot diff, so it needs a COMMIT — a correct fragment sitting in the working tree reports as missing.
- **release-ring-policy**: Several consecutive BETA releases are explicitly fine and NOT a backlog — an idea proves itself in the apps before the chain goes stable.
- **release-cut-runbook**: The release runbook: set skip-changelog BEFORE the check finishes — adding it afterwards needs a toggle, a re-run replays the old state.

## Full text

### `architecture-overview`

nexus-flow is an agent-native, offline-first suite: **the board (`nxf`), the memory (`nxm`) and the
channel (`nxc`) your agents work from** (and nothing else — not the agent, not brainstorming, not
quality gates). The public positioning is the README's (owner decision 2026-09-21, nxf 6j6v.psre):
an issue tracker for coding agents, with the memory and the channel beside it. The architecture is
`docs/specs/nxs-platform-foundation.md`; `docs/vision/nexus-flow.md` is the June vision, superseded
in parts (its own note says where).

**The `nxs` umbrella is the front door.** One **multicall binary** serves four personas, dispatched
by `argv[0]`:

- **`nxs`** — the umbrella: `nxs init` (pick which tools to set up + assemble the shared
  agent files), `nxs prime` (the fan-out you run by hand), `nxs guide`, `nxs
  migrate`/`doctor`/`status`, `nxs setup` (host integration), `nxs sync` (incl. the background
  daemon), `nxs mcp`, `nxs self-update`. `nxf`/`nxm`/`nxc` are personas of the *same* binary
  (`nxs flow …` = `nxf …`, `nxs memory …` = `nxm …`).
- **`nxf` (flow)** — the projects/tasks engine: items (the `type` is **plugin-declared**, not a
  core enum), dependencies + parent/contributes-to edges, due/defer, history + closing comment,
  and the derivation layer (ready/blocked/next as deterministic computation, not stored state).
- **`nxm` (memory)** — durable agent facts recalled across sessions (`remember`/`recall`/`forget`),
  its own `fact` op-log folded over the same substrate.
- **`nxc` (chat)** — the channel between you and your agents: `send --to`, `reply --thread`, escalation, channels
  and personas, with the agent sidecar compiled into the binary.

**THE CORE SUBSTRATE, one level down** (moved here on 2026-09-18 from [[build-test]], where an
architecture description had no business sitting): the production engine core is `crates/core`
(`nexus-flow-core`), and it is an **op-log CRDT substrate**. An append-only `ops` table is the
single source of truth; a write appends an op and folds it into materialized views (`items`,
`edge_adds`/`edge_removes`, `note_tombstones`, `notes`) with keep-if-beats LWW plus an
observed-remove OR-set. Derivation (`ready`/`blocked`/`next`) and the invariants are pure SQL over
those views — which is why the work list is always consistent and never needs repairing. The
bake-off that chose this design is `docs/specs/E0-sync-substrate-spike.md`, the model itself
`docs/specs/E1-core-data-model.md`. `automerge` is a **dev-dependency only** (the differential
oracle) and is never in the binary.

Modules **self-register** (`inventory`) into the roster `nxs init`/`prime` read, so adding a
product needs no umbrella change. One shared **`.nxs/` workspace** holds a single op-log CRDT
substrate db that every active module folds its own views over. The host runs **one SessionStart hook
per active module** (`nxf prime`, `nxm prime`, `nxc prime` — since nxf n2m6 + a2a1), not one
`nxs prime`.

- **Plugins** (per consumer, under flow): vocabulary mapping, ranking policy, the type system, and
  presentation — `issue-tracker` and `personal-todo` are bundled.
- **Consumers**: `manufakt.io` (coding-agent platform), `nexflow.it` (knowledge-worker PM). Both
  bundle the suite invisibly ("powered by nexus-flow").
- **Sync**: full offline-first — structure via a **hand-rolled, narrow relational CRDT on plain
  SQLite** (LWW + OR-set + tombstones), chosen by the E0 bake-off; **Automerge is kept as a
  differential-test oracle** (not in the binary). The prose body rides the **same LWW-longtext
  substrate field** and converges through the normal op sync — the earlier char-level Yrs/Y.Doc
  body backend was cancelled (2026-06-16) and Yrs is not in the binary. The server is the durable
  truth.

**Crate map** (the workspace members, re-verified 2026-09-18): `foundation` (shared substrate:
workspace/schema/manifest) · `core` (`nexus-flow-core` engine) · `facade` (the embedding API +
SemVer contract) · `cli` (the `nxf` surface) · `memory` (`nxm`) · `chat` (`nxc`) · `nxs` (umbrella
binary + library) · `nxs-init` (shared self-registration registry + agent-file assembler) ·
`nxs-ui` (presentation) · `guide` (`nxs-guide`, the one guide mechanism all blocks are served
through) · `sync` · `service` (the background sync daemon) · `server` (the relay) ·
`plugin-probe` · `test-support` · plus `xtask`. `examples/tauri-board/src-tauri` is deliberately
OUT of the workspace (an `exclude` entry, so CI never builds Tauri + WebKit) and is checked by its
own workflow.

The roadmap went `E0` spike → `E1` core → `E2` CLI → `E3` plugin system → `E4` sync → the **`nxs`
platform** (umbrella + memory + unified onboarding) → **nexus-chat**, which has shipped: its own
crate, persona, guide tree and embedded sidecar. This repo dogfoods the engine for its own issue
tracking (migrated off beads on 2026-07-06); run `nxs prime` (or `nxf next`) for the current entry
point.

### `priority-storage-canonical-ordinal`

Priority is a named plugin variant at the SURFACE but stored as the canonical ORDINAL.

Decision pivot: the label string was stored first, and that broke the gate asserting that the
canonical `--json` record is plugin-INDEPENDENT (`output.rs` never consults a plugin; only
presentation and ranking may differ). It is the faithful analogue of `vocabulary.status`, which
likewise stores a plugin-independent core token.

So: `--priority`/`--set` take a LABEL (`P0..P4` / `now..icebox`), resolved to its index in
`cfg.priority.labels` (`facade::write::resolve_priority`, which also accepts the canonical ordinal
key directly) and stored as that ordinal string; ranking is numeric on the ordinal;
`show`/`list`/`schema` map ordinal -> label via `cfg.priority.labels`; `--json` keeps the ordinal
(with additive `priority_label`/`type_label` fields for readers who want the display form).

NEVER store the label in the item record — it would make `--json` plugin-dependent.

THE GATE'S NAME, corrected 2026-09-18: this entry named `list_json_is_byte_identical_across_plugins`,
which no longer exists — a sentence that stays true while its pointer dies, exactly class 4 of
[[sweep-the-deleted-vocabulary]]. The live gate is
`list_json_is_plugin_independent_except_the_declared_type`
(`crates/cli/tests/guide_examples.rs`): it asserts the record is byte-identical across
`issue-tracker` and `personal-todo` once `type`, `priority_label` and `type_label` are removed —
the declared type being the one documented exception.

Related: `vocabulary.fields` gives plugin-named field headings for `show`/`schema`, with core
defaults in `default_field_label()`.

### `op-struct-external-constructors`

Changing the core `Op` struct (`crates/core/src/model.rs`) is NOT confined to `crates/core`:
`crates/sync/src/wire.rs` constructs `nexus_flow_core::model::Op { .. }` literals (in
`From<WireOp> for Op`, plus a test literal), gated behind the sync crate's `engine` feature.
Adding or removing an `Op` field there is a compile break, and `cargo test` builds the WHOLE
workspace — so always `grep -rn 'model::Op\|Op {' crates` (not just `crates/core`) before touching
`Op`.

Facade, CLI and server do NOT construct `core::Op` (the server has its own `WireOp`).

The wire envelope (`WireOp`) is the forward-compatibility seam: it must MIRROR new `Op` fields or
they are lost over sync. Verified 2026-06-20, and re-verified 2026-09-05 that the two `From`
implementations are still there.

### `nexflowit-plugin-is-proprietary`

The nexflow.it note/person/goal plugin is **proprietary IP and must NOT live in this repository**
(nexus-flow is the open-source side, nexflow.it is not). It is defined in `nexflowit-app`.

THE SEAM THAT MAKES THAT POSSIBLE NOW EXISTS — verified in the code on 2026-09-05, and this is the
part that used to be an open requirement:
`crates/facade/src/plugin/registry.rs` is a compile-time self-registration registry. Every plugin
— the two bundled here (`issue-tracker`, `personal-todo`) and any consumer's proprietary one from
ITS OWN crate — `inventory::submit!`s one `PluginRegistration { name, toml, order }`, where `toml`
is that crate's own `include_str!`. `plugin::load`, `plugin::plugin_names` and `plugin::available`
read that roster exclusively, so a consumer plugin appears purely by registering and linking: no
OSS source change, and its TOML never lands in this repo or on disk. A workspace picks its plugin
by name (`[flow] plugin = "…"`); an unknown name is a validation error. `order` is declared, so
the listing is deterministic rather than link-order accident. The old hardcoded `PLUGIN_NAMES`
const is still exported but `#[deprecated]` since 0.16.0 as a facade coexistence window — it can
only ever name the two plugins compiled into THIS binary, so migrate any pin to `plugin_names()`.

The mechanism mirrors the module roster one level up (`nxs_init::module`), which is the same
inventory pattern for whole products.

STILL WORTH CHECKING WHENEVER THE MCP SURFACE GROWS: `nxs mcp serve` must not assume a consumer
workspace or a consumer plugin — a host that connects gets whatever plugin that workspace
declares, and nothing in the OSS tree may special-case one. A separate, still-parked idea is a
programmatic trait layer for plugins; it is NOT the same thing as this registry and should not be
confused with it.

### `relay-ships-sqlite-and-postgres-not-dynamodb`

DECISION (owner, 2026-08-07): the SHIPPED `nxf-relay` binary carries SQLite + Postgres, NOT
DynamoDB. `release.yml` builds all four targets with `--features nxs-server/postgres` (verified
2026-09-05).

MEASURED, not estimated — a cold `--release` build of the relay alone: sqlite 76 crates / 57 s /
3.8 MB; +postgres 153 / 71 s / 5.0 MB; +dynamodb 247 / 3 m 35 s / 22.6 MB. DynamoDB pulls in
`aws-lc-sys` (native C/asm) and needs cmake plus a C toolchain on EVERY runner, to put ~19 MB into
EACH of the four archives — for a capability no archive consumer pulls: manufakt.io builds the
relay from a pinned revision (`apps/web/relay-pin.json`, tag+commit+features) with its own
toolchain and never unpacks ours. DynamoDB remains a SUPPORTED SOURCE BUILD and is documented as
such (spec §5.2, `nxf guide running-a-relay`, and a comment in the `[features]` block) — leaving it
out silently was the original mistake.

CONSEQUENT RULE FOR rustls IN THIS REPO: always depend on rustls with `default-features = false` +
`ring`, and name the provider explicitly via
`builder_with_provider(rustls::crypto::ring::default_provider())` (see
`crates/server/src/tls_pg.rs`). rustls defaults to aws-lc-rs — exactly the cmake dependency this
decision avoids — so it would otherwise come back in through the back door. Naming it is
additionally necessary because a `--features postgres,dynamodb` build compiles TWO providers in,
and `ClientConfig::builder()` then panics at runtime.

Proven: both musl legs cross-compile with postgres+rustls/ring through cargo-zigbuild (x86_64 and
aarch64, statically linked). The Postgres backend speaks TLS (webpki-roots, plus
`NXF_RELAY_PG_CA_FILE` for a private CA); `sslmode` still decides WHETHER TLS is used, so the CI
service container without SSL stays green unchanged.

OPEN AND DELIBERATELY NOT BRIDGED: the relay has NO CLIENT AUTHENTICATION. A managed store changes
nothing about that. That is also why the GHCR container image promised in spec §5.6 is still
waiting on the auth/multi-tenant slice — a one-command way to start the relay would be a
one-command way to put an unauthenticated shared board on the network.

### `the-running-binary-decides-the-service-instance`

Since nxf 6j6v.cvpy the precedence in `nxs_service::Instance::resolve_from` is THREE inputs, not two,
and the middle one is new:

1. `argv[0]` — an alias (`nexus-flow-dev`) wins outright. That is how a launchd-started service knows
   itself: `ProgramArguments` carries exactly one element, so it has no other channel. It is also the
   escape hatch for a human — `~/.nexusflow-dev/bin/nexus-flow-dev uninstall` addresses that instance
   from anywhere. The alias STANDS FOR `nxs sync daemon`, so the verb follows it directly;
   `<alias> sync daemon uninstall` answers `unrecognized subcommand 'sync'`.
2. `nxs_service::Origin` — where the running binary SITS. A build tree is recognised by the Cargo
   profile directory (`target/{debug,release}`, or one level below it where every test binary lives),
   by any `target` ancestor (a `--profile` of one's own), and by Cargo's own `CACHEDIR.TAG` checked by
   its SIGNATURE (a private profile inside a redirected `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`). Anything else is
   INSTALLED. Judged on the CANONICAL path — `Origin::ambient` goes through
   `program::running_program`, which canonicalises — because a service alias and every job the daemon
   spawns through it are symlinks that lie about where they live and tell the truth about what they
   are.
3. `NXS_SERVICE_INSTANCE` — for a BUILD only, and it says WHICH working copy's instance, never
   whether there is one. For an installed binary it is not read at all, not even to be validated.

WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE. Install a checkout's own service by running the BUILD
(`cargo build && ./target/debug/nxs sync daemon install`), never the installed `nxs`. An install
links the alias to the binary that ran it, so that is also the only way a development service ever
runs a development build. Five verbs say so when the variable named an instance they could not give a
vote to — `sync daemon install`/`uninstall`, `sync bind`, `sync unregister` and every `init` path —
out of one sentence, `nxs_service::instance_env_ignored_note` (the ambient form is
`ignored_instance_env()`), which lives beside `shared_workspace_note` for that function's own reason.

WHY, so nobody restores the old rule by accident: direnv exports the variable for a whole working
copy, so before this every call made while standing in one — the installed `nxf` on the PATH included
— was a call of the development instance. Measured on the owner's machine on 2026-09-05: all three
registered services pointed at the same `~/.local/bin/nxs`, so no development service had ever run a
development build. It also restored itself, because `sync bind` registers the service.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT DECIDES EVERY EDGE CASE: a false `Build` verdict only leaves the environment the
vote it had before this rule existed; a false `Installed` verdict silently moves a development build
onto the production registry. So every question `Origin::of` asks may only widen `Build`, and a
process that cannot name its own binary is `Build`.

FOR TESTS: a test binary is a BUILD (`target/<profile>/deps/…`), so the variable still decides for
any subprocess a test starts, and every `nxs_test_support` convention is unchanged —
`PinHome` clearing it, `pinned_home_env()` setting it to `nexus-flow`. The ignored-instance note is
`None` in every test for the same reason, so it cannot make a suite's output depend on the
environment its runner was started in.

### `branching`

**Always work on a `feat/`-style branch — NEVER commit to `main` directly**, unless the user has
explicitly allowed it for that piece of work. Branch *before* the first change:

```bash
git checkout -b feat/<short-slug>   # at the start of the work, off an up-to-date main
```

Work lands on `main` through a pushed branch + PR (the recent history is all PR merges). This is a
hard rule: if you find yourself on `main` with uncommitted work, create the branch first, then
commit. Explicit permission is per-task, not standing — ask again next time.

### `build-test`

WHAT THIS MEMORY IS, after 2026-09-18: the inventory of what CI runs, and the traps the local loop
cannot see. It no longer carries the local-gate policy — that is [[gates-run-in-ci-not-locally]],
which states the rule and the measurement (clippy NEVER locally; only the test file you changed,
plus `cargo fmt --all`) — and it no longer carries the engine architecture, which moved to
[[architecture-overview]]. The four commands `cargo test`, `cargo test --release`,
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are what CI runs FOR you; this
entry used to call them the fast local loop, and on this machine they are 88 to 122 minutes.

## What CI actually runs

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` is the source of truth. The `quality-gates` job, re-read from the file
on 2026-09-18, in order:

```bash
node --test                                 # the agent-sidecar suite; it has no cargo gate at all
# then: build the sidecar bundle (npm ci && npm run build) and export NXF_EMBED_SIDECAR=require
cargo fmt --all --check                     # --all, not just the default member set
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo xtask runners check                   # self-hosted routing stays off pull requests
cargo xtask macos-tests check               # every cfg(macos) test is in the macOS lane
cargo xtask platforms check                 # single-source drift gates: they fail on generated
cargo xtask channels check                  # content that somebody edited by hand
cargo xtask docs check
cargo xtask docs coverage
cargo test --no-fail-fast --test verb_seam \
  -p nexus-flow-cli -p nexus-memory -p nexus-chat   # the omission gate, named so it fails by name
cargo build -p nxs --no-default-features && clippy the same        # lean build 1
cargo build -p nexus-chat --no-default-features && clippy the same # lean build 2
cargo test --all                            # --all: `cargo test` alone misses other crates
cargo test --all --release                  # NOT on the pull-request event, see below
```

Seven jobs sit beside it: `platform-gates-windows`, `platform-gates-macos`, `macOS tests
(hosted)`, `postgres-parity`, `postgres-tls`, `managed-postgres`, `dynamodb-local`. Fourteen
workflow files in all; the ones with their own gate are `changelog-check`, `version-check`,
`facade-semver`, `example-check`, `install-sh-ci`, `install-update-smoke`, `npm-mcp-ci`,
`promote-ci`, `cache-sweep`, `content-ci`, plus `release`, `promote` and `publish-content`.
`cargo xtask changelog check origin/main` is the local form of the first.

**The release profile and macOS are staggered off the pull-request event.** `Tests (release)`,
`platform-gates-macos`, `macOS tests (hosted)` and steps inside `postgres-parity` and
`dynamodb-local` all carry `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'`: they run on every push to
`main` and to every `release/**` line, and on a manual `workflow_dispatch` — but not on the PR
event, where they were about half the machine time. Nothing that ships skips them (a release is
cut by tagging a commit on `main`/`release/**`), but a release-only break — classically a
`debug_assert!` with a side effect — reaches `main` before it reaches a reviewer. The
countermeasure is NOT a local full run; it is one `workflow_dispatch` of `ci.yml` on the branch
before the merge.

Also: `ci.yml` has a `concurrency` group that cancels superseded **PR** runs (never a
`main`/`release/**` push run) — a force-push mid-run cancels the old run by design, not a flake.
What that hides when it happens is in [[macos-ci-jobs-are-two-different-machines]].

**The two lean builds are the ones that actually bite**, because nothing in this repo links those
configurations: `crates/nxs` takes chat's default features, so the `default-features = false`
library variant — the one app-foundations embeds — has NO in-repo consumer and NO local gate. It
compiled only in CI, and it once stayed broken for a day behind six other green checks (`sha2`
moved onto the shared orchestration path while still gated behind chat's `cli` feature). Run at
least the lean builds before pushing anything that moves code between `cli.rs` and a shared
module, or that touches a `[features]` block — and never beside a running test suite
([[no-concurrent-lean-build-during-tests]]).

## The gate the local loop does not cover at all: `content-quality-gates`

`.github/workflows/content-ci.yml` is a SEPARATE workflow with no local counterpart, and it is
fail-closed. It bit on 2026-08-07: adding ONE guide topic in English went green through every Rust
gate and red there, because the website federates guides in **both** locales and asserts topic
parity (`assertTopicParity` in `content/lib/docs.mjs`).

There are **FOUR guide trees**, one per building block plus the umbrella — `crates/cli`,
`crates/memory`, `crates/chat`, `crates/nxs` — all served through the ONE mechanism in
`crates/guide` (`nxs-guide`) and fanned out by `nxs guide`. All four carry content. (The crate's own
description still counts three; 6j6v.b5he.)

Adding or renaming a guide topic touches these places (`<crate>` = `cli` | `memory` | `chat` |
`nxs`):

```
crates/<crate>/src/…/guide.rs           TOPICS       (the block's own list)
crates/<crate>/docs/guide/en/<topic>.md the EN page  (compiled into the binary)
crates/<crate>/docs/guide/de/<topic>.md the DE page  (website-only, but REQUIRED for parity)
crates/cli/tests/guide.rs               TOPICS       (FLOW ONLY — see below)
content/lib/docs.mjs                    BUILDING_BLOCKS[].order  (the site's list, by assertion)
crates/{chat,memory}/tests/golden/*.trycmd  (any ```console block the new page shows)
```

CORRECTED 2026-09-18: the fourth line is NOT a per-crate pattern, and reading it as one sends you
looking for a file that does not exist. Only `crates/cli` keeps a second, hand-written `TOPICS`
copy in its test. `memory` and `chat` guard the same drift differently, through
`tests/guide_examples.rs`: every ` ```console ` block in those guides — both locales — is held
against that crate's golden corpus, so changing a golden output without carrying the guides along
is red rather than a false map. memory's suite asserts the reverse direction too: every block in
`tests/golden/guides.trycmd` must be quoted by some guide, or that corpus drifts into a second,
unread test file.

The published slug is **`<binary>-<topic>`** (`nxf-getting-started`), never the bare topic: the
blocks share ONE docs page and its slugs are duplicate-free by contract. A cross-link between
guides must use that slug — `[core concepts](nxf-core-concepts)` — because the landing page
resolves a bare target only if it is a known slug and otherwise degrades the link to plain text
with no error anywhere. `checkCrossLinks` in `content/lib/docs.mjs` is what makes that a red
build instead.

Plus `TRYCMD=overwrite cargo test -p nexus-flow-cli --test golden` for `guide.trycmd` (and
`-p nxs` for the suite fan-out, `-p nexus-memory` / `-p nexus-chat` for that block's guide listing
AND its worked session). Build `nxs` FIRST in every case — the freshness gate refuses to burn a
stale binary's output into a golden, and it fires on a guide `.md` edit too, because the `en` tree
is a build input. Run the content gate locally before pushing:

```bash
(cd content && npm ci && node --test && node assemble.mjs \
   && node validate.mjs --schema schema/content-contract-v1.json)
```

## The stale-binary trap (`cargo test -p <crate>`)

`nxf`/`nxm`/`nxc` are **`argv[0]` symlinks** to the single `nxs` binary (since the multicall
collapse). `nxs` is its own package that depends on the persona crates — not the reverse — so
**`cargo test -p <crate>` never builds it**: the run compiles every test binary, finds
`target/<profile>/nxf`, follows the symlink, and executes an *arbitrarily old* `nxs`. It goes
green while asserting against code you did not write. This is not theoretical — goldens once
regenerated against a pre-rebase binary silently deleted a command from the agent-facing docs and
cost hours of chasing a phantom.

A **gate catches this** (`crates/test-support`): the golden harnesses call
`nxs_test_support::assert_multicall_binary_fresh()` and a `binary_freshness` test in cli/memory/
chat fails if `target/<profile>/nxs` is older than any source that links into it — under
`TRYCMD=overwrite` it aborts *before* trycmd can write. So the rule is enforced, not remembered:

```bash
cargo build -p nxs && cargo test -p nexus-flow-cli   # the fast loop, made honest
cargo test --all                                     # builds nxs itself — always safe
```

One thing the gate does NOT cover: **`cargo test -p <crate>` does not compile other crates' test
files.** A broken callsite in `crates/facade/tests/read.rs` stayed invisible across several green
partial runs. Only `cargo test --all` compiles them all.

(Guide docs — `crates/{cli,memory,chat,nxs}/docs/guide/en/**`, embedded via `include_dir!` — used
to live here as a trap: "touch `guide.rs` to force a rebuild". That was a misdiagnosis. A guide
*content* edit rebuilds on its own — the macro expands to `include_bytes!`, which rustc records in
dep-info — and each of those crates' `build.rs` emits `rerun-if-changed=docs/guide/en` so add and
remove are tracked too. That last part matters most when a tree GROWS: an added or retired topic
is an ADD or a REMOVE, exactly the case dep-info cannot see. The `en` trees are first-class build
inputs the stale-binary gate watches; `de` is website-only and stays out.)

## Build cache

`target/` grows unbounded — cargo never auto-prunes stale incremental and dep artifacts, and it
has reached tens of GB more than once. Two levers:

- **Slimmer debug info** is already wired in the workspace `Cargo.toml`: `[profile.dev] debug =
  "line-tables-only"` roughly halves `target/debug` while keeping file:line backtraces. It does
  not touch `debug_assert!` / `cargo test --release` (those gate on `cfg(debug_assertions)`, a
  separate knob). Nothing to run — it applies on the next build.
- **Prune by SIZE, not by age.** `cargo sweep --time 15` is the obvious call and it is the WRONG
  one here: churn on this workspace is roughly 60k files a day (parallel sessions, debug+release
  double builds, feature variants), so almost nothing is older than 15 days and the sweep reclaims
  nothing. Use `cargo sweep --maxsize <GB>` instead — see
  [[slow-tests-check-target-deps-and-swap]], where that was measured. Never sweep while a build or
  test is running, and prefer it over `cargo clean`, which forces a cold rebuild.

### `conventions-patterns`

- **TDD for all behavior** (test-first); scaffolding and config (Cargo.toml, release profile) are
  exempt.
- **CLI contract:** `--json` everywhere, deterministic output (agent ergonomics is the measuring
  stick).
- **A new CLI verb needs a counterpart on the library seam.** One shared core, with the CLI and an
  app over it as equals, is specified per module (the embedding-host API specs for flow, memory and
  chat) and now *enforced*: the verb-seam gate (`crates/{cli,memory,chat}/tests/verb_seam.rs`,
  engine in `crates/test-support`) walks each clap tree and fails on any verb with no matching
  public symbol on that module's `Engine`/facade. Both lists are derived, so the gate cannot drift;
  what you declare is only the difference, and every entry carries a reason — `CliOnly` (host-own:
  `init`, `agent-manifest`, `self-update`, import/onboarding), `Alias` (on the seam under another
  name — the gate checks the target exists), or `KnownGap`, which names a board item. This is
  precisely what the three parity differentials structurally cannot see: they compare what exists on
  both seams and are blind to a verb that exists on only one.
- **WHAT `KnownGap` ACTUALLY MEANS TODAY, measured 2026-09-18** — this entry used to say "a real
  omission, with the board item that tracks it. A gap without a ticket is not a waiver", and that
  is not what the one live entry is. There is exactly ONE `KnownGap` in the repository: chat's
  `tick`, naming `6j6v.dvyq`, which is CLOSED — closed because it recorded a DECISION ("NO SEAM
  TWIN BY DECISION, not by omission"), not because anybody forgot it. So the word carries two
  states, an omission somebody owes and a settled question, and only opening the item tells them
  apart. Do not read a closed item behind a `KnownGap` as rot, and do not tighten the rule to "the
  item must be open" — it would fail the only correct entry. 6j6v.pqww carries the fix (a
  `ByDecision` variant, so the gate can enforce what this rule claims). Until it lands: when you
  declare a `KnownGap`, name an OPEN item, and say in one line whether you mean an omission or a
  decision.
- **Every PR with user impact needs a changelog fragment**: a `changes/<slug>.md` with EN **and** DE
  body sections and frontmatter `type: added|changed|fixed|removed`. The `changelog-check` CI gate
  enforces it on the PR and is fail-closed; validate locally with
  `cargo xtask changelog check origin/main`. Only PRs with **no** user impact (internal infra/CI,
  docs, tooling) opt out: one that touches only never-shipped paths passes by itself (6j6v.c37e),
  anything else gets the `skip-changelog` label instead of a faked fragment. See
  `docs/specs/release-management.md` §4.2, `changes/README.md`, and [[changelog-scope]] for what
  counts as impact.
- **The `crates/facade` public API is a SemVer contract** (§4.3-§4.5): a **patch never breaks it**
  (no removed/renamed/signature-changed `pub` items) — a break belongs on a **minor** (the break
  axis in 0.x). The `facade-semver` CI gate (`cargo xtask facade semver-check`, cargo-semver-checks)
  enforces it fail-closed on a patch bump; flag a facade-touching fragment with
  `facade: changed|breaking` (+ `security: true` for a security fix). Security fixes backport to
  the current + 2 previous minor lines — see `docs/specs/maintenance-and-backports.md`.

---

### `changelog-scope`

Changelog fragments (`changes/*.md`) feed `release-notes.json` and the self-update notes.

SCOPE (set 2026-06-18 by the owner, superseding an earlier CLI-only rule): the measuring stick is
**PRODUCT IMPACT**, not "touches the CLI". A fragment is required for

  (a) user-facing CLI changes, AND
  (b) notable engine/library capabilities of the product — for example the embedding-host API in
      the `nexus-flow-facade` crate.

Rationale: a deliberately shipped feature (a whole epic) must not vanish from the release feed just
because it is not CLI surface. The earlier rule — "the CLI is the only thing that needs a
changelog" — held until an entire embedding-host epic closed with no headline entry;
`docs/specs/release-management.md` §4.3 now states the product-impact scope explicitly.

TWO EXEMPTIONS, and neither is served by a faked fragment. Where the PR touches ONLY paths that never
ship (the `NO_PRODUCT_IMPACT` allowlist in `xtask/src/changelog.rs`: docs/ minus
docs/architecture and docs/generated, CI workflows minus every workflow that can publish (a test
keeps that list in step), tests, xtask minus the gate's own changelog.rs/facade.rs, repo prose incl.
README.md, which rides in the tarball but is prose), the gate passes BY ITSELF since 6j6v.c37e — needed because a fork contributor
cannot set a label. Everything else takes the `skip-changelog` LABEL, set by a maintainer:

1. NO PRODUCT IMPACT: the landing site (`site/**`: robots/sitemap/SEO/copy/styling), infra and CI,
   docs, internal refactors, and purely internal performance work with zero consumer-visible
   behaviour change.
2. NEVER PUBLICLY SHIPPED (owner, 2026-06-21): a fix that only affects a version which never
   shipped publicly or as stable — a behaviour that only ever ran under a beta or pre-release tag.
   The user never saw the change, so there is nothing to tell them. Worked example: a fix to the
   keyed-map form of the priorities config, whose array predecessor had only ever run in one 0.5.0
   pre-release and never reached the stable feed.

See [[conventions-patterns]] for where this sits among the other PR rules, and
[[release-cut-runbook]] for why a RELEASE PR is red by construction and needs the same label for a
third, purely mechanical reason.

(Absorbed `changelog-skip-unreleased` on 2026-09-18 — it was exemption 2 above, in a memory of its
own, linked from here as "the second exemption".)

---

### `no-concurrent-lean-build-during-tests`

In nexus-flow, never run `cargo build -p nxs --no-default-features` (the lean variant) **at the same
time** as `cargo test`. The lean build overwrites `target/debug/nxs` with an MCP-less binary, and
the MCP integration tests in `crates/nxs/tests/mcp.rs` spawn the REAL binary via
`assert_cmd::cargo_bin("nxs")` over stdio. If the lean binary is on disk when those tests run, they
all fail with `error: unrecognized subcommand 'mcp'` — which looks like a code break but is just a
clobbered artefact.

**Why:** debug and release use separate profile directories (`target/debug` vs `target/release`), so
`cargo test --release` is safe to run alongside `cargo test`. But two `cargo` invocations that both
write `target/debug` (a default-features test plus a no-default-features build) race on the same
`nxs` artefact.

**How to apply:** run feature-variant builds serially with the test suite (let one finish before
starting the other), or build the lean variant into a separate `--target-dir`. After any
`--no-default-features` build, the next plain `cargo test` / `cargo build -p nxs` restores the
MCP-enabled `target/debug/nxs`.

The same collision bites two SESSIONS sharing one checkout, not just two commands — see
[[review-session-in-a-shared-checkout-mistakes-the-work-for-its-own]].

---

### `det-ids-env-test-race`

`NXF_DETERMINISTIC_IDS` (read by `nxs_foundation::workspace::deterministic_ids_enabled()`, used by
chat/flow/memory `mint_id`) is a **process-global env var**. A unit test that does
`set_var`/`remove_var` on it (for example chat's
`deterministic_ids_are_sortable_and_stable_under_the_switch`) races any **parallel** test in the
same test binary that mints ids and asserts a **positional** order — the flag can flip between two
`post_message` calls, so one id is a ULID and the next an `m-<seq>`, inverting their sort order.

**Why it hides:** it passed under `cargo test` (debug) by scheduling luck but went red under
`cargo test --release` (different parallel timing) — a classic release-only flake. It was hit
during the nexus-chat app-facade work: `messages_in_channel_returns_full_rows_in_id_order` asserted
`[m1, m2]` and failed once in the release gate.

**How to apply:** in tests that check "ordered by message_id", never toggle the env and never assert
a hardcoded position — capture the returned ids and assert against `sorted(captured)` (which holds
under any minting scheme), and check row content by `.find(|r| r.body == …)`, not by index. Only
the single-purpose determinism test should touch the env, and it must assert against its own
store's ids (per-store counts do not cross-contaminate). Always run `cargo test --release` before
trusting an order-sensitive test — see [[slow-tests-check-target-deps-and-swap]] and
[[facade-watch-test-flaky]].

---

### `engine-seam-test-rule`

A new public library seam (`Engine::*`) is NOT done without a test AT THAT SAME SEAM. CLI coverage
does not count for it: tests going through `facade::*` or an `nxm`/`nxf` subprocess exercise the
path the PRODUCTS DO NOT TAKE — manufakt.io and nexflow.it speak `Engine::*`.

Three review rounds in a row (2026-08-03 and 2026-08-04, across the memory-classification work, the
retrieval-rule work and the MCP/NEXUS_MEMORY.md work) produced exactly this as their heaviest
finding: the CLI thoroughly tested, the engine seam not at all.

Whoever adds a new engine command writes the test for it in the same move —
`crates/memory/tests/embed.rs` is the designated place on the memory side.

The same blindness produced a worse failure elsewhere: a sync driver was proven by parity tests
running in plain `#[test]` threads, which have no async runtime, while the shipped binary ran it
inside one and crashed on the only path there was. See
[[sync-postgres-driver-needs-off-runtime]] — "thoroughly tested on a path the product does not
take" is the same shape.

An open board item tracks the gate that would enforce this mechanically; until it stands, this rule
carries the load. (The related verb-seam gate already exists and catches a different omission — a
CLI verb with no seam counterpart at all — see [[conventions-patterns]].)

### `nxc-sidecar-ships-with-the-binary`

The nxc agent sidecar has been COMPILED INTO the `nxs` binary since v0.54.0 — not placed beside it
any more.

WHY: the place-it-beside route has a bootstrap hole that no version can close from the inside — the
code that places the second file lives in the NEW version, but the update is always carried out by
the OLD one. Every machine on 0.51.0 or earlier therefore ended up without a sidecar, and the fix
that was meant to ship it never effectively reached the installed base.

FORM: `agent-sidecar` bundles via esbuild into ONE self-contained ESM file
`dist/nxc-agent-sidecar.mjs` (~1.4 MB); `crates/chat/build.rs` compiles it into the binary with
`include_bytes!`, and `worker.rs` unpacks it on first use into
`<cache>/sidecar/<sha256[..16]>/nxc-agent-sidecar.mjs` (`NXF_CACHE_DIR`, else
`XDG_CACHE_HOME/nxf`, else `~/.cache/nxf` — the same ladder as `selfupdate.rs::cache_dir`).
Resolution order in `installed_sidecar()`: `NXC_SIDECAR` (developer override) -> EMBEDDED ->
`sidecar_beside(exe)` (legacy installs at 0.53.0 and earlier, plus the source tree's `main.mjs`
under `target/{debug,release}`). Content-addressed means binary and sidecar are a pair by
construction, which retires the whole "they carry no common version" problem outright. The tarball
has TWO members again (`nxs`, `nxf-relay`); `install.sh` and `selfupdate.rs` only place a separate
sidecar when a `--version` pin selects 0.52.0/0.53.0, and otherwise REMOVE a superseded copy.

TRAP 1: `build.rs` is tolerant (no bundle -> `None`) so a contributor without Node can build.
`NXF_EMBED_SIDECAR=require` is what turns that tolerance off — and it is set in exactly TWO PLACES,
not pipeline-wide (measured 2026-09-18, correcting this entry's earlier "ci.yml AND release.yml set
it", which read like a guarantee over every job): `ci.yml`'s `quality-gates` job, exported to
`$GITHUB_ENV` right after the bundle-build step, and `release.yml`'s `build` job, as a step-level
`env:` on the two binary-build steps. The other six ci.yml jobs never build the bundle at all and
rely on `build.rs`'s documented fallback to the source tree. So the rule is: wherever a job builds a
binary that MUST be able to start an agent, build the bundle first and set `require` — otherwise you
get a binary that installs cleanly and cannot start an agent, and nothing in that job says so.

TRAP 2: because the bundle has no `node_modules` beside it, the Claude Agent SDK cannot resolve its
native `claude` binary itself — the HOST resolves `claude` on `PATH` and passes it as
`spec.claudePath`. `is_bundled_sidecar()` keys on the FILE NAME, which is why the unpacked file
keeps exactly that name and only the directory carries the hash.

TRAP 3: SIX places must spell the file name identically, and the gate
`every_place_that_ships_the_sidecar_spells_it_the_same` (`crates/chat/tests/worker.rs`) counts
OCCURRENCES, not files: `agent-sidecar/package.json` 1, `crates/chat/build.rs` 2, `install.sh` 4,
`release.yml` 2, `ci.yml` 3, `crates/cli/src/selfupdate.rs` 1.

TRAP 4: NEVER `npm ci --omit=optional` for the bundle build — that also skips esbuild's
integrity-pinned `@esbuild/<platform>` package.

---

### `never-review-your-own-work-order`

THE REVIEW IS NEVER STARTED BY THE IMPLEMENTING AGENT. Whoever received a coding assignment (for
example through a `pm-next-task` brief) must NOT invoke `review-pr` / `/nxf-workflow:review-pr`
themselves — not "just to be safe", not even when the quality gates are green and the pull request
is open. Owner instruction of 2026-08-07, explicit and without exception.

The review is started by the owner or the PM in their OWN, FRESH session: only a session that did
not write the code can read it without prejudice — one that built it re-checks its own assumptions
and will fail to notice in exactly the places where it already failed to notice while building.

What the implementing agent does instead: open the pull request, report the state honestly
(including the open points), and offer the handover.

CONSEQUENCE FOR `.nxf/status.jsonl`: `review_requested` and `review_completed` are written by the
REVIEW session, not by the coding session. A `review_requested` entry set by the coding session is
wrong and belongs removed (it happened once and was taken out again).

HOW TO GET HOLD OF A FINISHED REPORT: do not start reviewers yourself — look in `.nxf/review/`, or
resolve the last `review_completed` entry via `pm-work-status`, which carries the `report_path`.
That is exactly what went wrong on 2026-08-07: the owner's report was already sitting in
`.nxf/review/` while the coding session was spinning up reviewers of its own in parallel.

See also [[review-session-in-a-shared-checkout-mistakes-the-work-for-its-own]] for the failure on
the other side of this rule.

---

### `sync-postgres-driver-needs-off-runtime`

TRAP: the SYNCHRONOUS postgres driver (crate `postgres` 0.19, with r2d2/r2d2_postgres) owns its OWN
tokio runtime and calls `block_on` on the CALLING thread. In an async context tokio then panics
with "Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime" — and in a DESTRUCTOR that becomes an
unwindable abort (SIGABRT).

CONSEQUENCE, discovered 2026-08-07: the relay's Postgres backend had NEVER worked in the `nxf-relay`
binary. `main` is `#[tokio::main]`, so `NXF_RELAY_BACKEND=postgres` already broke at boot in
`backends()`, and every axum handler would have done the same. Not on a rare path — on the only
one.

WHY NO TEST SAW IT: `crates/server/tests/postgres_parity.rs` calls the trait from plain `#[test]`
threads, which have NO runtime at all. The parity was genuine and the binary was dead anyway.
Exactly the same blind spot as the engine-seam findings: thoroughly tested on a path the product
does not take (see [[engine-seam-test-rule]]). Anyone hanging a sync driver behind an async server
MUST write a test that runs INSIDE a runtime context — `tests/postgres_in_runtime.rs` is the
template (multi-thread, current-thread, and an embedded relay over real HTTP).

THE SOLUTION IN THE REPO: `store_pg::off_runtime(f)` picks the context in which blocking is allowed
— `block_in_place` on multi-thread, a scoped OS thread on current-thread (where `block_in_place` is
itself forbidden), and directly when there is no runtime. From a `spawn_blocking` thread
`block_in_place` is demonstrably fine (unit-tested). EVERY entry point is wrapped: `connect`,
`append`, `read_since`, `register`. AND — easy to forget — the DROP: `PoolHandle(Option<PgPool>)`
hands the pool to `off_runtime` in `Drop`, because closing the connections is the same blocking
driver call, and a clean shutdown otherwise became a SIGABRT.

The DynamoDB backend never had this problem: `store_ddb::block_on` bridges via its own bridge
runtime plus a channel, with the same flavour switch. Anyone building a third backend copies one of
the two patterns — not neither.

---

### `handover-lists-are-themselves-unverified`

When an item hands over a list as it closes ("these N artefacts must move together when X is
closed"), THE LIST ITSELF is unverified — and in this repository it has already been wrong twice
in a row.

PROVEN CASE (2026-08-14/15, during the nexus-chat surface recut): the item that introduced
`reply --escalate` closed by announcing that THREE artefacts would have to move together when the
`summarize` escalation gap was closed — the characterisation test, the doc comment on
`ChatStore::last_reply_escalated`, and the EN+DE clause in `changes/reply-escalate.md`. The
successor item moved all three and reported truthfully that it had moved all three.

THERE WERE FIVE, and the number grew at EVERY inspection:
- The review found a FOURTH: `set_escalated`'s private doc comment, in the very module that
  performed the closure.
- The post-review found a FIFTH: the PUBLIC rustdoc on `route_declared_channel_completion`, whose
  predicate had described a bug ever since.
The corrected list was thus itself still one short — and this memory said "four" in its first
version, under-reporting the very incident it documents. Caught by the branch review on
2026-08-15.

WHY THIS IS ITS OWN CLASS OF ERROR: the implementer was EXACT with respect to the list they were
given. Their report was true. An artefact still survived that tells readers the opposite of the
code. No test, no gate and no careful report catches that — the check "did I work through the
list" cannot, by construction, answer "was the list complete". And as the corrections show, even
"I derived the list once more" does not answer it either.

WHAT TO DO WHEN YOU INHERIT SUCH A LIST: do not work through it — DERIVE IT AGAIN. The cheap route
is a search for the TERM of the gap across `src`, `tests`, `changes/` and `docs/`, then compare the
result with the inherited list. The difference is exactly what would otherwise have stayed behind.
PUBLIC doc comments first: they are the most expensive place to be wrong, because they are a
contract, and in this case they were at the end of the chain.

AND IF YOU WRITE SUCH A LIST: ship the SEARCH you derived it with, not just its result. A list with
its derivation is checkable; one without is an assertion. Better still: hand over no list at all,
but the SEARCH TERMS — that is what the third item in this chain did, and the review confirmed it
explicitly as the right application of the lesson rather than an omission.

Related but not the same: the rule against lifetime- rather than turn-scoped predicates (same
session, four occurrences) concerns the code; this one concerns the HANDOVER. Its code-side twin is
`RESERVED_HANDLE_PREFIX`, where a list was replaced by a CLASS RULE after being wrong for a round —
the same lesson, cast in code.

---

### `gate-evidence-is-per-commit`

A gate result (tests, lint, changelog check) proves EXACTLY the tree it ran against — and "the
tree" is HEAD **plus the working copy**, not HEAD alone.

During the nexus-chat surface work (August 2026) SIX independent gate runs were lost, and each
loss had its own shape:

- One run was raced by a concurrent second `cargo test` (the documented env-var race class).
- One ran while an implementer was editing sources — the binary-freshness guard tore it down.
- One was overtaken by a commit: HEAD moved in the middle of the suite.
- One reported 24 failures that were pure artefacts.
- One `changelog check ok` was TRUE AND WORTHLESS: the gate reads `git diff <base>...HEAD`, so only
  committed state, and the fragment under test was in the second-to-last commit of the range. The
  green run happened BEFORE the fragment was committed and never saw it.
- One run had a guard that compared only HEAD — the implementer edited the working tree without
  committing, so HEAD stayed equal and the guard said nothing.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE, in both directions:
- Before starting a gate run, check that no implementer is holding the tree.
- Before commissioning work that changes the tree, check that no gate run is in flight.
- The run logs HEAD AND the number of dirty files at the start and at the end, and PRINTS ITS OWN
  VERDICT (VALID / VOID), rather than leaving two numbers for somebody to compare who never will.
- A gate runs ONCE, at the end, against the state you are reporting — not behind every commit.
  That is both the expensive form and the only probative one.

A red run out of a race is NOT evidence of anything — reading it as a finding is the same mistake
as believing a green that checked nothing.

---

### `sweep-the-deleted-vocabulary`

Whoever REMOVES something cannot search for the identifier that no longer exists. The text that
survives is the text describing what USED to be there. So: **search the vocabulary of what was
DELETED, not of what remains.**

During the nexus-chat surface work (August 2026) stale text showed five distinguishable shapes,
and each needed its own search:

1. Field enumerations in brace form — `{thread_id, acted, reason, ...}`.
2. THE SAME enumerations in PROSE — "the four fields `ReplyReceipt` reports".
3. COMPLETENESS CLAIMS — "the ONLY place an app can learn this", "the WHOLE result of the
   forwarding". This shape is found only by searching for the claim, never for the field.
4. A statement that is TRUE but points at a renamed or non-existent test. Neither a search over
   changed identifiers nor one over deleted vocabulary finds it — the text is right, only the
   pointer is dead.
5. THE WORK ORDER ITSELF. A brief to an implementer contradicted itself because one step had been
   updated and the matching "not your job" list had not. The document that says what to do is under
   the same staleness discipline as the code.

THREE BLIND SPOTS WHERE SEARCHES FAIL — they produced the heaviest findings:
- **Files the search never opened.** Mechanisable as `vocabulary ∖ changed files`.
- **Lines DIRECTLY BESIDE edited lines.** A hunk moves line 4; line 3 carries the same untruth on.
- **An addendum that scopes itself too narrowly.** A note saying "read `roles/` as the new path
  below" makes the spot LOOK HANDLED while the actual removal beside it stays undocumented.

AND A TRAP IN THE CLEANUP ITSELF: a pass that compares each file against `HEAD` sees its own
earlier round as "unchanged" and skips it. Compare against the BRANCH BASE, not HEAD — otherwise
you quietly declare your own work to be somebody else's.

A tool for this lives at `xtask/sweep-retired-vocabulary.sh` — explicitly A REVIEW AID AND NOT A
GATE (it exits 0 either way and is not in CI). On its first run it found three places that two
careful manual passes had missed, including a removed flag in LIVE source.

---

### `a-test-name-is-a-claim`

The NAME of a test is a claim about its body — and it can be false without anything going red.

Twice during the nexus-chat surface work (August 2026):

- `stream_is_refused_to_a_persona_and_says_what_to_do_instead` promised the second half in its own
  name and checked NONE of it. That is exactly why a verb the same commit had removed from the
  surface survived in the message.
- `each_member_thread_names_its_own_assignee_with_no_tie_break_left_to_lose` claimed no tie-break
  was left. In the scenario as built, even a BROKEN outer guard produced byte-identical output,
  because the inner one already excluded that session. Both guards were redundant there.

THE ONLY CHECK THAT FINDS THIS IS MUTATION: remove the mechanism the test claims to check and see
whether the test goes red. If it stays green, it is checking something other than what its name
says.

THIS APPLIES TO MUTATIONS THEMSELVES. Twice a mutation made nothing red, and both times the reason
was in the setup rather than in the subject:
- The release path called a `pub(crate)` twin function while the mutation hit the `pub` shell that
  no production code used any more.
- A prescribed assertion pinned the STATE a predicate reads instead of the predicate FIRING —
  closing the door left the state untouched and the test green.

A mutation that makes nothing red is not proof of correctness; it is a finding about the test.

---

### `a-relayed-claim-becomes-yours`

Whoever hands work to implementers and passes their reports on becomes the AUTHOR of every claim
they let through. **A claim you cannot re-run is not evidence — and one you pass on becomes your
own.**

Three times during the nexus-chat surface work (August 2026), every time from the coordinating
side:

- An implementer reported that a cleanup sweep was "mechanised and checks itself". The
  coordinator declared that the best result of the round and reported it onward — without looking.
  It did not exist: a one-off shell pipeline described in prose, with no recorded vocabulary list,
  not repeatable. (In the following round the tool was actually built, and it immediately found
  three missed places.)
- A reviewer wrote that a certain scenario was "never built". Passed on without checking. A
  pre-existing test did build it; the finding was real, but considerably NARROWER than described.
- A number from an older log entry ("the known five lines") was carried into a work order without
  re-running it against the current state. It was one.

THE SECOND HALF OF THE SAME DISCIPLINE: A PRESCRIBED FIX IS A HYPOTHESIS, NOT AN INSTRUCTION.
Twice a solution dictated by the coordinating side was wrong, and only mutation showed it:
- An assertion pinned the STATE a predicate reads instead of the predicate FIRING.
- A proposed discriminator would have opened exactly the bug the implementer then covered on their
  own — their simpler anchor was STRONGER, not merely equivalent.

So prescribed corrections go out as a hypothesis, with an explicit invitation to test them and
report counter-findings rather than route around them. An implementer who refutes the coordinator
is the procedure working.

---

### `the-board-is-local-and-not-in-git`

This workspace's board is **fully git-ignored** and does NOT travel with the code: `nxf
close`/`create` write locally only, there is no "push the board" step at the end of a session, and
no sync stream is bound (`nxs doctor`: `sync: not bound`, measured 2026-09-18) — the board is
single-device. If you want to share the state, share it through the PR, not through the board.

WHERE IT ACTUALLY LIVES, and the shorthand hides it: `.nxs` in the repo root is a SYMLINK to
`~/.nxs-workspaces/nexus-flow/`, so the database is `~/.nxs-workspaces/nexus-flow/db.sqlite` and
sits outside the repository tree altogether. It is ignored twice over regardless — the repo
`.gitignore` names `.nxs`, and the workspace directory carries its own `.gitignore` of `*`. The
practical consequence of the link: a `git clean`, a fresh clone or a worktree does not touch the
board, and two checkouts of this repo pointing at the same link share ONE board.

The item types are declared by the plugin (`issue-tracker`: `bug|chore|decision|epic|feature`) —
**there is no `task`**. `nxf schema` names the set this workspace actually accepts.

Everything else about the board — the verbs, the core rules, this workspace's id prefix, the
session close — is in `nxf prime` and therefore does not belong here.

---

### `handover-notes-are-not-durable-memory`

Handover notes for the next session belong in the `session-handover` skill, NOT in durable
memory.

**Why:** durable memory is reserved for long-lived project knowledge. Carsten corrected me when I
parked a "what comes next in this plugin epic" note there. Where a session left off is a different
kind of information and has its own mechanism.

**How to apply:** when a session ends, write the handover through the `session-handover` skill.
Durable memory stays for facts worth recalling across many future sessions — not for "where I
stopped".

---

### `shell-evaluates-long-descriptions`

A TRAP WHEN CREATING BOARD AND MEMORY ENTRIES FROM THE SHELL: `nxf create --description "..."` and
`nxm remember "..."` in DOUBLE quotes let the shell evaluate the text before `nxf`/`nxm` ever sees
it. In this repository that is not an edge case but the normal case: descriptions constantly quote
identifiers in backticks and placeholders in angle brackets.

PROVEN 2026-09-02 while creating a board item: `nxc reply --thread <id> "..."` became "the human
types ." — the shell read the angle brackets as a redirection. And the word `nxs guide` in
backticks became the COMPLETE OUTPUT of `nxs guide`, written into the middle of the item
description. The command reported "created" and looked successful; only the two lines
"(eval):1: no such file or directory: id" before it gave it away. Anyone who does not read back
never notices.

THE FORM THAT HOLDS — a quoted heredoc inside a command substitution, which leaves the body
literal:

    nxf create --type feature --title "..." --description "$(cat <<'EOF'
    Text with `backticks`, <placeholders> and $variables stays untouched.
    EOF
    )"

The single quote around EOF is the decisive part; without it the shell evaluates the heredoc body
just the same. Passing a file is equally safe: `"$(cat body.md)"` does not evaluate its contents.

REPAIR, if it has already happened: `nxf update <id> --set description="$(cat <<'EOF' … EOF
)"` — `description`, `design` and `completion_criterion` are ordinary `--set` fields. For `nxm` the
same form with `nxm remember --key <key>`, which replaces the entry in place.

READING BACK IS PART OF THE STEP: after every create/remember with a longer text, run
`nxf show <id>` or `nxm recall <key>` once and check that what you wrote is what is there. See
[[nxm-remember-has-no-stdin-dash]] for the neighbouring trap on the same surface.

---

### `gates-run-in-ci-not-locally`

MEASURED 2026-09-03 against a real pull request and the transcript of the session that built it.
Not a feeling — numbers.

## The finding

    CI, wall clock until everything is green   7.5 min   (second run 7.2 min — stable)
    Locally, one full gate cycle               88 / 100 / 27 / 122 min
    Factor                                     12 to 16

Four full local cycles in one night = 5.8 h. CI would have done the same work four times in half
an hour, and not on this machine.

The machine is the floor: Intel i5-8257U @ 1.4 GHz (4 cores, a 15 W mobile chip from 2019), 16 GB
RAM, swap in use, and the checkout sits on an external USB disk formatted HFS+ rather than APFS.
Creating 2000 small files — the shape of a Rust build — takes 30.4 s there against 5.6 s
internally.

## The rule

1. WHILE WORKING, test narrowly: `cargo test -p <crate>`, `--test <file>`. In the measured
   transcript such runs had a median of ~30 s. That is also exactly the TDD inner loop.
2. PUSH EARLY and let CI be the gate. 7.5 min, in the background, on somebody else's hardware.
3. AT MOST ONE full local run, and only for what CI does not see on a pull request.

This agrees with [[gate-evidence-is-per-commit]]: "a gate runs ONCE, at the end, against the tree
you are reporting — not behind every commit."

## What CI does NOT see on a pull request

Everything carrying `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'`: `Tests (release)`
(`cargo test --all --release`), `platform-gates-macos`, the `macOS tests (hosted)` job, and steps
inside `postgres-parity` and `dynamodb-local`. Verified against `ci.yml` again on 2026-09-18.

CORRECTED 2026-09-05: this memory used to say that `#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]` tests run
NOWHERE in CI. That is no longer true. There is now a dedicated `macOS tests (hosted)` job
(`cargo build -p nxs`, then `cargo test --no-fail-fast -p nxs -p nexus-chat -p nxs-service` on a
hosted macOS runner) and a `cargo xtask macos-tests check` gate in `quality-gates` that fails when
a `cfg(macos)` test is not in that lane. What remains true is only the staggering: that job, like
the release profile, is skipped on the pull-request event.

Everything else needs no local run. CI does considerably MORE than the local four: fmt, clippy
-D warnings, `cargo test --all`, six xtask drift gates, the sidecar suite under node, two lean
builds, Windows platform gates, postgres-tls, postgres-parity, managed-postgres and
dynamodb-local. The full inventory, in order, is in [[build-test]].

## The evidence that is stronger than the arithmetic

The session behind that pull request ran `cargo test --all` FOUR times, all green — and CI still
found a real bug: a test asserted a bound that only holds on macOS and fell over on Linux. Four
full local runs did not prevent that and COULD not, because they never covered the missing
operating system. Locally green says nothing here about CI green.

## Relationship to the TDD skill

No conflict at the core, but two sentences that are easy to misread:

- "Verify RED — watch it fail" is UNTOUCHED and still mandatory. It is a targeted run of seconds,
  not a suite run. This memory is NOT a licence to skip the red step.
- "Verify GREEN — other tests still pass" and the checklist item "All tests pass" must NOT be read
  as a local `cargo test --all` per cycle. CI supplies that assurance here.

## The one full run belongs BEFORE the merge — via workflow_dispatch

MEASURED 2026-09-03 over the last 20 ci.yml runs:

    PR run      7.2 - 10.2 min   (quality-gates is the pole: 7.4 min, of which 281 s `Tests (debug)`)
    main run   17.1 - 28.1 min   (quality-gates 17.0 min — almost all of the difference is `Tests (release)`)

Because of the pull-request staggering, **the first time the full set runs is AFTER the merge.**
That was defensible while the house rule was "run `cargo test --all --release` locally first" —
and that countermeasure is exactly what this memory repeals. Without a replacement a release-only
break goes red on `main`, blocks the version cut through `ci-green` in `release.yml`, and needs a
fresh pull request.

THE REPLACEMENT COSTS NO YAML: `ci.yml` already has `workflow_dispatch`, and a run triggered that
way is NOT `pull_request` — so the release tests and the macOS lane come along.

    After mitigating the review findings, after the last push, BEFORE the merge:
    dispatch ci.yml on the branch once and wait for green.

Once per work order, not per push. Cost ~13 min, once. Gain: `main` does not go red, the release
is not blocked, and a release-only break surfaces while it still belongs to a pull request.

A dispatch is also the ONLY way to get macOS coverage on a feature branch, because a PR run renders
both macOS lanes `skipping` — confirmed on PR #478. And a dispatch cancels nothing: `ci.yml`'s
`cancel-in-progress` is `${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}`, evaluated on the run being
QUEUED, so dispatching beside an open PR is safe (counter-measured over three dispatches on PR
#465, one of them two seconds after the PR run started — all six runs completed `success`).

This does not work on a fork PR (nobody can dispatch there) — which becomes relevant the moment
the repository is made public.

## NEVER `cargo clippy` LOCALLY — MEASURED 2026-09-18, and it cost a day

The rule above ("test narrowly, CI is the gate") was in place and STILL a subagent-driven run of
eight tasks spent about fifteen hours of wall clock on local gates, because "the four commands"
was read as a list to shorten rather than a habit to drop, and because the CONTROLLER's dispatch
prompts told every implementer to re-run a list of neighbouring suites plus clippy.

    cargo clippy -p nexus-chat --all-targets -- -D warnings    15 - 25 min, EVERY time
    the same clippy in CI's quality-gates job                   part of a 7.5 min run

It is not a shorter run than `cargo test`; it type-checks the crate AND every test target again.
On one task it ran five times — once per fix round, twice more because the 10-minute tool timeout
moved it to the background and it was reissued.

THE RULE, owner instruction of 2026-09-18:

1. DO NOT run `cargo clippy` locally at all. Not `-p <crate>`, not `--all-targets`, not "once at
   the end". CI runs it on every pull request and fails the run; that is the whole assurance.
2. Run ONLY the test file(s) covering the code you just changed (`cargo test -p <crate> --test
   <file>` / `--lib <module>`), plus `cargo fmt --all`, which costs seconds.
3. Do NOT re-run neighbouring suites "to be safe". A cross-suite break is what CI is for.
4. A DELEGATING SESSION PUTS THIS POLICY IN EVERY SUBAGENT PROMPT, VERBATIM — not in some of them,
   not only in the ones carrying a quality-gates envelope. A fresh implementer with Bash reaches
   for clippy on its own because every code-quality habit it has says to, and a general-purpose
   subagent told only to REVIEW will run cargo unprompted "to corroborate" a source-level finding
   unless it is told not to. The same applies to the no-cargo constraint in a SHARED checkout,
   where a concurrent run also destroys the other session's build
   ([[no-concurrent-lean-build-during-tests]]).

WHAT THIS BUYS, measured on the same run: after the policy changed, a fix round went from hours to
the length of its own test file.

(Absorbed `no-cargo-constraint-must-reach-every-subagent` on 2026-09-18 — it was point 4 above in a
memory of its own, and this one already quoted it.)
