### `review-session-in-a-shared-checkout-mistakes-the-work-for-its-own`

A review session started in the SAME checkout as the coding session can mistake itself for the
author of the code under review and refuse the review, citing
[[never-review-your-own-work-order]].

MEASURED 2026-09-05 on the pull request for the escalation-parking feature: a freshly started
review session declined the assignment with "this is my own work from today". Its evidence: the
reflog showed a commit plus two amends from today on exactly the commit under review, and the board
item already carried detailed design notes on exactly the points to be reviewed.

BOTH PIECES OF EVIDENCE ARE PROPERTIES OF THE SHARED WORKING DIRECTORY, NOT OF THE SESSION'S
MEMORY. A fresh session in an existing repo always finds somebody's recent commits there. The
fallacy is natural and it is structural: the session has no access to the other's transcript but
sees its traces in the file system.

WHAT RESOLVES IT, in this order:

1. ITS OWN TRANSCRIPT. If you do not remember writing the file, you did not write it. This is the
   only check the session alone can make, and the decisive one.
2. `ps`. Two separate PIDs with separate start times; commits created AFTER the review session
   started cannot be its own if it has done nothing since. The review session ran this itself and
   thereby confirmed the correction independently — exactly right: do not cave on assertion, look.
3. WHO COMMISSIONED IT. The rule forbids the IMPLEMENTING agent from starting the review. An
   assignment issued by the owner and merely relayed by the coding session is the intended form,
   not a circumvention of it.

WHOEVER COMMISSIONS A REVIEW SESSION says this UP FRONT — otherwise it costs two rounds. And they
say the second half straight away, which the session cannot see by itself: BOTH SHARE ONE
`target/`. Two concurrent cargo runs in it destroy each other (see
[[no-concurrent-lean-build-during-tests]]). The review session should read the diff and take the
gate results from `gh pr checks <pr>`, not start `cargo test --all` alongside.

THE CLEAN SOLUTION if this recurs: start the review session in its own git worktree instead of the
shared checkout. Both problems disappear at once — the confusion and the `target/` collision.

---

### `the-project-language-is-english`

The project language is English. Everything this repository writes down and keeps is English:
ticket titles and descriptions, memories, commit subjects and bodies, PR titles and descriptions,
issues, code, comments and documentation.

THE ONE EXCEPTION IS THE LIVE CONVERSATION. An agent talks to a human in that human's own language
— the owner works in German, and answering him in English would be worse, not more correct. The
exception ends the moment something is written down: what goes onto the board, into a memory, into
a commit or a PR is English, no matter which language produced it. That is the boundary that used
to blur — German conversations produced German tickets by drift, never by decision.

VERBATIM STAYS VERBATIM. Code identifiers, file paths, CLI flags and commands, proper names and
established technical terms are never translated. Without this exception a language rule makes
things worse, because it invites translating the very names that have to match the code.

TWO SURFACES ARE BILINGUAL ON PURPOSE and stay that way: the user guide (`docs/guide/de` and `/en`
in every guide-carrying crate) and the changelog fragments under `changes/` (EN and DE per
fragment, gated by `changelog-check`). That is a product decision for German-speaking users, not
sloppiness. Nobody "cleans it up" by deleting the German half.

THE HISTORY STAYS GERMAN, AND THAT WAS DECIDED. Commits and PRs written before this rule are German
and remain so. Keeping the history was decided on 2026-07-12, after weighing a full history rewrite
before going public: rewriting messages changes every commit id, and consumers pin git tags —
engine-bridge and agent-runtime in app-foundations, `Cargo.lock` in three repos, over a hundred
tags in this repo including the first stable, plus the changelog's PR references. Translating the
history retroactively is the same operation as discarding it, at the same cost. English applies
from this rule forward, and CONTRIBUTING says so in one sentence.

OPEN TICKETS AND MEMORIES ARE ENGLISH FROM HERE ON. Anything created from now on is English. An
open item you touch — editing a field, adding a note — moves over while you are there. Closed items
are historical record and stay as they are. (The durable memories were migrated wholesale on
2026-09-05: every surviving entry is English, body and introduction.)

WHY IT MATTERS NOW: this repository goes public. A newcomer reads the board, the memories and the
log; German artifacts either turn them away or hide the reasoning that makes this project worth
reading in the first place.

THE ENFORCEMENT IS MEANT TO LIVE IN CONFIG, NOT IN WILLPOWER: an open board item designs a
`ticket_language` setting — an imperative directive in prime, the same directive at the write
point, and a corrective post-op check, with the verbatim exception mandatory. Until that ships,
this memory carries it.

---

### `a-tickets-own-measurement-is-unverified`

A MEASUREMENT WRITTEN INTO A TICKET IS EVIDENCE THE TICKET CARRIES, NOT EVIDENCE YOU HAVE. Re-run
it before you act on it — and before a REMOVAL, always, because a removal has no identifier left to
grep for afterwards.

PROVEN CASE (2026-09-05). A chat item had been re-cut from a decision into a chore on the strength
of a measurement taken on 2026-08-25 and pasted into its description, layer by layer:

    read_cursors   only consumer: ChatStore::inbox (store.rs:853)

That line is why the item said mark_read "advances a cursor nothing evaluates any more" and why
removing the whole unread apparatus looked free. It was wrong. ChatStore::read_cursor_seen was a
second reader, and it fed ChatStore::opener_wake -> PrimeReport::wake -> prime --json's
threads_you_opened — the app-seam record that a completed board left EXACTLY when the cursor passed
its completing reply. Strike the table and no board could ever leave that list again.

WHY THE ORIGINAL MEASUREMENT MISSED IT, because the lesson is in the mechanism and not in "be more
careful": a grep for the TABLE name finds both readers. What the measurement did was stop at the
first consumer it could explain. inbox was the obvious one, it accounted for the symptom the item
was about, and the trace ended there instead of following EVERY accessor's own callers one level
further. A named getter beside the table is the shape that hides: it reads like a helper, not like
a consumer.

THE CHEAP CHECK THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT, and it needs no judgement:

  1. For each thing to be removed, list its ACCESSORS (functions that touch it), not its textual
     hits. Then list each accessor's own callers, transitively, until you reach a public surface.
  2. Read the ticket AGAINST ITSELF. A removal ticket usually carries two lists — "what is removed"
     and "what stays untouched". This one had both, and its own "stays untouched" list named
     facade::opener_wake, which read something on the removal list. A ticket that contradicts
     itself has not finished being designed, and that is visible without opening the code.

WHAT TO DO WHEN THE RE-RUN COMES OUT OTHERWISE: hold, report, and leave the finding as a RUN rather
than a paragraph — a test that goes red the moment somebody attempts the removal, so the next
attempt is told what it costs instead of discovering it in a consumer. Then correct the claim
wherever the repository repeats it: the false sentence had also been copied into the gate
read_surface.rs, where it read as settled fact.

HOW IT ENDED, and the ending is the other half of the lesson (2026-09-08, nxf 6j6v.4d2z). The
removal landed three days later, and NOT because anyone re-argued the measurement: the consumer the
gate found was REPLACED first. nxf 6j6v.2hx9 derived the session-start notice from the OPERATION —
what finished since the caller's previous session ended — so the cursor lost its second reader by
being made unnecessary rather than by being declared unimportant. Only then did read_cursors,
mark_read, facade::inbox and the PrimeReport catch-up fields go, in one change, with the four-surface
gate re-run first and green. So the holding pattern is: hold, pin the finding as a run, build the
replacement, re-measure, then remove. The pinning file was retired WITH the apparatus it guarded,
which is correct — a gate whose subject is gone is itself a false map — and the account of what it
held now lives in read_surface.rs's module doc.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MAKES THE FINDING USABLE: that measurement was right about one thing and wrong
about the other, and the two are easy to say in one breath. NOBODY CALLS mark_read (true, measured
over five layers). NOTHING READS THE CURSOR (false at the time). Unused is not unread. Only the
second would have made the removal free; the first is an argument for giving the write a caller —
and when nobody wanted to write that caller either, it became the argument for removing the write.

RELATED, AND NOT THE SAME: [[handover-lists-are-themselves-unverified]] is about a list handed over
at CLOSING time ("these N artefacts must move together"). This one is about a measurement embedded
in an OPEN ticket as its justification. Same family — an inherited claim becomes yours the moment
you act on it, see [[a-relayed-claim-becomes-yours]] — different artefact, and this one is more
dangerous because it reads as data rather than as a reminder.

---

### `nxm-remember-has-no-stdin-dash`

NXM AND NXF DO NOT SPELL "READ FROM STDIN" THE SAME WAY, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS SILENT.

`nxf note add <id> -` and `nxf create --description -` read the body from STDIN. `nxm remember`
does NOT: its `<TEXT>` is positional, so

    nxm remember - --key k --introduction '...' < body.md

stores the literal string `-` as the whole memory, reports `remembered k`, and lists the key in the
index with its introduction. The BODY is one hyphen and nothing says so. Caught on 2026-09-05 only
because `NEXUS_MEMORY.md` is committed and the regenerated diff showed an empty section — an agent
that does not review that diff loses the fact entirely, at exactly the moment it was trying to make
it durable. An open board item tracks giving `nxm remember` the same STDIN form `nxf` has.

UNTIL THEN, pass the body as an argument:

    nxm remember "$(cat body.md)" --key k --introduction '...'

and then ALWAYS verify with `nxm recall <key>`. One command, and it is the only thing that can tell
you the write landed.

TWO MECHANICAL DETAILS THAT BITE WHEN SCRIPTING THIS:
- A body that begins with `- ` (a markdown list) is parsed as a FLAG. Put the option arguments
  first and separate the text with `--`: `nxm remember --key k --introduction '...' -- "$BODY"`.
- `"$(cat file)"` is safe, but a bare double-quoted literal is not — the shell evaluates backticks
  and angle brackets inside it first. See [[shell-evaluates-long-descriptions]].

### `aws-account-ids-never-in-the-repo`

TWO RULES THAT OUTLIVED THE INFRASTRUCTURE THEY WERE LEARNED ON. The `infra/` tree was deleted
from this repository on 2026-08-23 when the delivery stack moved into the nxsflowcom accounts (it
now lives in `nxsflow-landing-page`), but both of these are properties of the accounts and of the
release workflows this repo still owns.

1. **NEVER write an AWS account id into code, a pull request, or the git log.** This repository is
   going public, and the git history is being kept rather than rewritten, so an id committed today
   is an id that is published forever. Account ids are supplied at RUNTIME from the GitHub secrets
   `NXS_STAGING_ACCOUNT_ID` / `NXS_PROD_ACCOUNT_ID`; tests and fixtures use the documented example
   id `123456789012`. This is why the release workflows address the other account purely by
   convention (`nxs-<env>-release`, `nxs-<env>-artifacts-<account>`) and needed no edit when the
   accounts changed.

2. **A TRUST ANCHOR IS DEPLOYED BY HAND, never by a workflow.** A workflow cannot create the role
   it assumes — that is a bootstrap circle, not a policy preference. So the role a deploy workflow
   assumes is applied manually and verified against live IAM in each account; only what it can
   already assume belongs in automation.

See [[oidc-no-repository-owner-condition]] for the trust-policy condition that breaks such a role.

### `declared-members-bare-caller-qualified`

A declared channel's `members:` are recorded BARE (`dev`) while every caller's own identity is
QUALIFIED (`<origin>/<actor>`, e.g. `yyb8/dev`). `ensure_declared_channel` materialises the bare
members plus the qualified AUTHOR of the send, and nothing else.

So any comparison of a caller handle against a declaration MUST go through
`facade::same_identity` (origin-blind: equal, or the qualified identity's bare tail) — never `==`
and never a SQL `WHERE handle = ?` join. A string-equality comparison silently answers "not a
member" to every member that has not itself SENT to the channel, which reads as an empty result
rather than as an error.

Found twice, and cheaply the second time only because the first was written down: 6j6v.v39s (the
thread gate, where the doc comment described a bare-only comparison the code never did) and
6j6v.cs03 (`nxc search` answered "no matches" to every declared member that had only ever replied —
including for its own words).

WHERE THE ONE RULE LIVES NOW, re-measured 2026-09-18 because this entry used to name the wrong
file: the rule is `facade::declared_seat` (`crates/chat/src/facade.rs:1147`) and its two readers are
`require_thread_readable` (through `is_channel_member`) and `facade::search` (through
`searchable_channels`). `ChatStore::search_messages` is NOT one of them any more and says so in its
own source — "WHO may search WHAT is not decided here any more" (`store.rs:2400`): it takes a
channel list that `facade::search` has already resolved. Anyone adding a third reader resolves the
scope in the facade and hands the store a list, rather than teaching the store the rule a second
time.

### `flock-ends-at-the-last-close-not-the-holders`

An `flock` does NOT end when the holder closes its descriptor. It hangs off the OPEN FILE
DESCRIPTION, and the kernel drops it only when the LAST descriptor referring to that description
closes. `fork` — and `posix_spawn`, which is how `std::process::Command` starts every child on macOS
— copies the whole descriptor table, so a child that has been forked and has not yet reached
`execve` holds a second reference to it. `O_CLOEXEC` closes it there, but not before.

So in ANY multi-threaded process that also spawns children, this is a race:

    let f = File::open(p)?; flock(f, LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB); ... drop(f);   // releases NOTHING, sometimes
    let g = File::open(p)?; flock(g, LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB);                // EWOULDBLOCK

THE RULE: always `flock(fd, LOCK_UN)` in an explicit `Drop` before the descriptor closes. That
releases the lock on the description itself, so letting go depends on the holder and on nothing else
in the process. The kernel's release-on-last-close stays the backstop for paths that run no
destructor (a crash, `SIGKILL`), so nothing about crash safety is lost.

MEASURED on macOS on 2026-09-07 (nxf 6j6v.1zs2), 100 000 acquire/close/acquire cycles per row, with
one thread spawning `/usr/bin/true` beside them:

    spawners  release        re-acquire refused   first acquire refused
    0         close only     0 / 100 000          0 / 100 000
    1         close only     165 / 100 000        2 139 / 100 000
    3         close only     372 / 100 000        6 520 / 100 000
    1         LOCK_UN+close  0 / 100 000          0 / 100 000
    3         LOCK_UN+close  0 / 100 000          0 / 100 000

Remove `O_CLOEXEC`, so the child holds the copy for its whole life rather than until `execve`, and
the first-acquire refusal rate goes 2.1% -> 29%: the window is the fork-to-exec gap and nothing else.

WHERE IT BIT: `nxs-service`'s `ServiceLock` and `RegistryLock` both left release to the close, and
both module docs stated the false version as fact. It surfaced as `macOS tests (hosted)` answering
PASS/FAIL/FAIL/PASS on one identical tree — the neighbouring test in that same binary spawns
`sleep 30`. Both now carry an explicit `Drop`.

HOW TO TEST IT deterministically, without a race: `dup` the holder's fd, drop the holder, then try to
acquire. `dup` and `fork` both add a reference to the same open file description, so `dup` reproduces
every time what a fork reproduces 165 times in 100 000.

### `claude-agent-sdk-scoping-airgap`

claude-agent-sdk subagents inherit the user's GLOBAL config (including MCP servers such as
Playwright) and can reach the web via Bash even when `ClaudeAgentOptions`
`tools=[...]`/`allowed_tools=[...]` are set — `bypassPermissions` auto-approves MCP and network.

Discovered in a tool-scoping spike: agents in the restricted arm browsed the web via Playwright-MCP,
contaminating the very experiment that was measuring tool scoping.

To truly air-gap a scoped agent:
- `setting_sources=[]` (do not load user/project/local settings → no inherited MCP),
- `strict_mcp_config=True` together with `mcp_servers={}`,
- `disallowed_tools=['WebFetch','WebSearch']`,
- and strip `curl`/`wget`/`gh` from the env `PATH`.

Verify by grepping the transcripts for `mcp`/`playwright`/`browser`/`webfetch`/`http` tool calls —
an air gap you have not checked for is an assumption, not a control.

Also: do NOT wrap the batch in `perl -e 'alarm N; exec ...'` — it leaves SIGALRM at `SIG_DFL` and a
stray signal kills python mid-run (exit 142). Run python directly and rely on `max_turns` plus
resumability.

### `parallel-worktree-agents-race`

Launching two `Agent` calls with `isolation: "worktree"` in the SAME message (concurrently) raced:
one subagent's `git checkout -b <branch>` executed against the SHARED main checkout instead of its
own worktree, flipping the main checkout off `main` (its worktree stayed on the auto
`worktree-agent-<id>` branch). This is the "worktree isolation can collapse into branch switching in
a shared checkout" trap Carsten warns about for diamond/parallel phases.

**Why:** concurrent worktree creation plus an in-agent `git checkout -b` is not reliably cwd-pinned
to the agent's worktree at launch time.

**Safe recipe for parallel worktree subagents:**
1. **Stagger** the launches — launch agent A, confirm its worktree via `git worktree list` (main
   still `[main]`), THEN launch agent B. Do not launch both in one message.
2. Give each agent a **hard-abort preflight**: verify `git rev-parse --git-dir` !=
   `--git-common-dir` AND that `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` is under `.claude/worktrees/`; if
   not, STOP and run nothing.
3. Tell agents **never** to `git checkout` / `checkout -b` / `switch` — work on the
   isolation-provided `worktree-agent-<id>` branch and report the final commit **SHA**.
4. **Collect by SHA** (merge or cherry-pick the reported SHA onto an integration branch), since the
   worktree and its branch may be auto-cleaned when the agent finishes.
5. After each launch, re-check `git worktree list` and that `git branch --show-current` on main is
   still `main`.

Verified working for a two-task parallel diamond in the nexus-chat milestone work. A shared
checkout has a second, independent failure mode worth reading alongside this one:
[[review-session-in-a-shared-checkout-mistakes-the-work-for-its-own]]. See also
[[the-board-is-local-and-not-in-git]].

### `golden-harness-runs-in-crate-dir`

The trycmd golden harness (`crates/cli/tests/golden.rs`) runs `nxf` in the **`crates/cli` working
directory, not a sandbox**. That is why `crates/cli/.nxs` exists on disk: a real workspace, seeded
with the fixed identity `NXF_DETERMINISTIC_IDS` hands out (prefix `ab12`), ignored twice over — by
the repo-level `.gitignore` entry `.nxs` and by its own generated `.nxs/.gitignore` containing
`*`. (It was called `.nexusflow` before the workspace directory was renamed; anything still saying
so is stale.)

CONSEQUENCE: a golden case for a command that PERSISTS state OUTSIDE the workspace and has no
reset step is not reproducible across runs — `nxf setup claude` writes `.claude/settings.json`, so
the first run reports `hook_added: true` and the next `false` — and it also leaves an un-ignored
artifact behind. Such host-config commands are listed in `EXEMPT` in `xtask/src/docs.rs` (as of
2026-09-05 that list is exactly `["setup claude"]`) and are covered by hermetic `TempDir`
integration tests instead. Note that host setup now lives on the umbrella — `nxs setup` is the
canonical verb and `nxf setup claude` delegates to it.

TWO GUARDS THE HARNESS GREW SINCE, both of which a new golden suite needs as well:

- **It pins `$HOME`.** A golden corpus asserts stdout AND stderr byte for byte, so anything the
  binary reports about the developer's own machine — a dangling program alias, a background
  service registration — would fail every case, and under `TRYCMD=overwrite` would be burned into
  the committed goldens, developer paths and all. `nxs_test_support::pinned_home_env()` supplies
  the pairs.
- **It refuses a stale binary FIRST.** `nxs_test_support::assert_multicall_binary_fresh()` runs
  before trycmd touches a single case, because a package-scoped run leaves `nxs` unbuilt and an
  old binary under `TRYCMD=overwrite` would rewrite the goldens from stale output. See
  [[build-test]] for the whole stale-binary trap.

The clock is pinned too (`NXF_NOW`), because `close`/`archive` stamp their timestamps from `now`
and would otherwise capture the live wall clock.

### `facade-watch-test-flaky`

A full `cargo test --all` (debug OR release) occasionally goes red on a `nexus-flow-facade` test
from the **delete-and-recreate family** — a test that throws away the workspace db at the SAME path
and recreates it, and therefore depends on both file-system event timing and SQLite locking under
parallel load.

THIS IS A CLASS, NOT A SINGLE TEST. This entry named only one until 2026-09-01, and that is
precisely what it nearly failed on: the next occurrence was a different test.

Proven occurrences:

- `--test watch` :: `detects_same_path_db_delete_and_recreate` (2026-07-10). A file-system watch
  test; foreign changes were in the tree, so not change-induced.
- `--test engine` :: `subscribed_reads_repoint_after_a_recreate_on_the_watcher_cadence`
  (2026-09-01, `cargo test --all --release`). DIFFERENT SYMPTOM, same causal family:
  `NxfError { kind: Io, msg: "failed to set sqlite pragmas: database is locked" }` out of the
  `ws.open_store()` in the test's OWN helper `recreate_db_with` (`crates/facade/tests/engine.rs`),
  not out of the subject. Searching for the word "watch" does not find this one.

**Why it is a flake, and how to PROVE that rather than assert it:** green when repeated in
isolation (3/3), green for the whole crate alone (`cargo test -p nexus-flow-facade --release`), and
green in CI `quality-gates`. Both times the red run happened in a tree whose change did not touch
`crates/facade` at all.

**How to apply:** if a full run reds on ONLY a test from this family, then (1) repeat that test in
isolation, (2) run the whole crate in isolation, (3) only then judge — and repeat the full run once
if you intend to report a clean gate result ([[gate-evidence-is-per-commit]]: a red run out of a
race proves nothing). Do not attribute it to your own diff without having done those three steps. A
real fix would be to serialise the delete-and-recreate tests instead of letting them race against
the same file in parallel.

### `slow-tests-check-target-deps-and-swap`

**THE BASELINE FIRST, because the diagnosis below is only meaningful against it.** The checkout
lives on an external USB disk formatted HFS+ (it used to be internal, APFS, PCIe). Measured:
creating 2000 small files takes 30.4 s there against 5.6 s internally (5.4x) — exactly the shape
of a Rust build. A full `cargo test --all` cycle is therefore **regularly 88 to 122 minutes**.
That is the NORMAL CASE, not a symptom. Anyone who starts counting files in `target/debug/deps`
because a run passed an hour is hunting a problem that is not there. The real consequence of this
baseline lives in [[gates-run-in-ci-not-locally]]: full gates do not belong on this machine at
all.

DIAGNOSE ONLY WHEN IT GETS SUDDENLY MUCH SLOWER THAN THAT BASELINE, or when the disk is genuinely
filling up. On 2026-07-09 a full `cargo test` took >1h45m at a time when minutes were normal: each
CLI integration-test binary ran 2-10 min at ~0 CPU, stuck in uninterruptible disk wait. Two
compounding machine-level causes, neither of them the code:

1. `target/debug/deps` had ballooned to **901,522 files / 36+ GB**. The accumulation was NOT
   months old — nothing in it was older than 15 days, because churn here is roughly 60k files a
   day (parallel sessions, debug+release double builds, feature variants). **That is why
   `cargo sweep --time 15` cleans NOTHING here and `cargo sweep --maxsize <GB>` is the right
   lever** (2026-07-09: reclaimed 37.6 GiB; note it may empty `debug/deps` entirely while keeping
   newer release artifacts, so the next debug build is cold). Never sweep while a build or test is
   running.
2. The Mac was swap-bound: 11.7/12 GB swap used, the data volume 92% full (~18 GB free) so swap
   could not grow; load >20; `XprotectService` had burned 161 h of CPU, most likely rescanning the
   mass of freshly built binaries.

HOW TO APPLY: when a build or test here is *unbelievably* slow, do not debug the tests first — run
`/bin/ls -f target/debug/deps | wc -l` (use `-f`; a sorted `ls -lt` itself takes minutes at that
size) plus `sysctl vm.swapusage` and `df -h /System/Volumes/Data`. Also: piping a background test
through `tail -N > log` hides all progress (a 0-byte log until EOF) — poll with `ps` showing the
current `target/debug/deps/<test>-<hash>` child instead.

SPOTLIGHT IS THE ONE MITIGATION THAT KEEPS GETTING LOST. `target` was once a symlink to
`target.noindex` precisely so Spotlight would skip it. That arrangement did not survive the move
to the external disk: as of 2026-09-05 `target` in the main repo is an ordinary directory,
`target.noindex` does not exist, and the volume is indexed. Restoring it means recreating the
symlink (never a plain `target/` dir) or turning indexing off for the whole volume with
`sudo mdutil -i off`. Local git excludes for both names live in `.git/info/exclude`.

### `launchd-install-is-not-home-isolated`

A pinned `$HOME` isolates files but NOT launchd. `nxs sync daemon install` does write its plist
under `$HOME/Library/LaunchAgents`, but it then calls `launchctl bootstrap gui/<uid>` — and that
domain is the developer's REAL login session, whatever `$HOME` says. A black-box test that actually
runs the install path therefore bootstraps a real agent into the session of the human running it,
pointing at a test binary in a `TempDir` that is about to disappear.

THIS HAPPENED ONCE AND COST FIVE DAYS: the production sync clock on this machine stood still from
30 August to 4 September, because launchd held a registration for `com.nxsflow.nexus-flow` from a
deleted `TempDir` and the real plist could not displace it.

SINCE THAT FIX THIS MEMORY IS A CHECK, NOT AN ADMONITION. `nxs_service::launchd::RealCtl` can only
be constructed through `RealCtl::for_login_session()`, which refuses with `forbidden` when the
process's `$HOME` is not the home directory the user database holds for `getuid()`.
`install_for`/`uninstall_for` construct it FIRST, before plist, alias and log directory. A test with
a pinned `$HOME` now gets a named refusal instead of a silent poisoning; the counter-proof lives in
`crates/nxs/tests/no_test_reaches_the_real_launchd.rs`.

THE GAP THAT REMAINS: a test that does NOT pin `$HOME` is indistinguishable at runtime from a human
typing the command — it still reaches launchd. An open board item proposes a gate that would
enforce `$HOME` pinning for black-box tests; this refusal is not that gate.

SO, STILL: no test in this repo runs the real install. `sync bind` tests all pass `--no-daemon`;
`nxs init` tests use `--no-service` or no flag at all. The yes-branch is proven at a trait seam
(`background_service::Machine`, `sync::mod::Autostart`), not at the process. Anyone building a new
surface that can install needs the same seam — otherwise the test is not isolated, merely not yet
executed.

AND IF IT DOES HAPPEN, SOMETHING SAYS SO NOW: `nxs sync daemon status` compares the loaded
registration (`launchctl print gui/<uid>/<label>`, field `path`) against its own plist and reports
a foreign or orphaned one as `registration: FOREIGN — ...` with path and cause, instead of letting
it pass as a stale heartbeat.

---

### `nxs-init-writes-the-real-registry`

`nxs init` WRITES to the background service's workspace registry (`~/.nexusflow/workspaces.toml`,
or `~/.nexusflow-<name>` under `NXS_SERVICE_INSTANCE`) — on every run, `--json` included. That
makes every black-box test that runs `nxs init` and does NOT pin `$HOME` a leak: it leaves one dead
`TempDir` entry per case in the developer's REAL registry. That is how the 98 corpses measured once
came about; while implementing the change that introduced the write, two full test runs had already
added 77 new ones.

It does not show up locally (nothing goes red) and in CI not at all (there `$HOME` is a throwaway
directory anyway) — the same fail-open shape as the earlier bug where ten tests pinned `HOME` to a
`TempDir` but inherited `NXS_SERVICE_INSTANCE` from the environment.

RULE: every test that starts `nxs init` pins `$HOME`. `nxs_test_support::cargo_bin` already does
this; if you build your own command (to avoid inheriting that helper's defaults), add
`.pin_home(nxs_test_support::pinned_home())` — `pinned_home()` is public for exactly this. The
tests that were affected were `crates/nxs/tests/{e2e,retrieval_rule,the_session_start_ceiling,
a_persona_gets_the_suites_prime}.rs`.

THERE IS NO GATE THAT ENFORCES IT: the existing `every_pinned_home_pins_the_instance` gate only
checks that a PINNED home also pins the instance, not that anything is pinned at all. An open board
item tracks closing that hole.

### `linux-process-start-is-reconstructed`

A process start time is RECONSTRUCTED on Linux, not reported, and must therefore never be checked
against a wall clock to the millisecond.

`crates/service/src/heartbeat.rs::process_started_at` has two implementations. macOS/iOS reads the
instant DIRECTLY from `proc_bsdinfo` (`pbi_start_tvsec` + `pbi_start_tvusec`) and hits the real
`execve` to the microsecond. Linux computes it: field 22 of `/proc/<pid>/stat` is ticks since BOOT,
and the boot instant comes from the `btime` line of `/proc/stat` — in WHOLE SECONDS. The
reconstruction can therefore be about a second away from the real start, in either direction.

CONSEQUENCE FOR TESTS: an assertion like `process_started_at(kind) >= instant_before_the_spawn`
passes on the Mac and fails on Linux. That happened on 2026-09-03 in the work on the daemon status
report: locally on macOS all four gates green, `quality-gates` on the Linux runner red — and both
times the code the test accused was correct. If you bound a start time against the wall clock, give
the bound at least two seconds and write the reason beside it.

CONSEQUENCE FOR PRODUCTION: none. `born_together` allows a stamp LATER than the process start
without limit, and an earlier one by `START_TIME_SLACK` (60 s) — sixty times more room than this
reconstruction can be off. Two readers on the same machine also compute the same result (`btime` is
stable), so comparing two reconstructions is exact.

---

### `cfg-split-kills-the-callee-elsewhere`

Splitting a function into two versions with `#[cfg(target_os = ...)]` can KILL A DIFFERENT
function — on exactly the platform you are not building on.

MEASURED 2026-09-04 while fixing the launchd poisoning bug: `registration_line` was split into a
macOS version (which calls `describe_registration`) and a non-macOS version (which returns `None`).
That left `describe_registration` unreachable from anything outside macOS. `-D dead-code` (implied
by `-D warnings`) turned `quality-gates` (ubuntu) AND `Platform gates (windows-latest)` red — while
BOTH macOS lanes stayed green and `cargo clippy --all-targets` on the developer machine said
nothing.

WHY NOTHING SHOWS UP LOCALLY: on macOS the function is reachable, and `--all-targets` additionally
pulls in the `#[cfg(test)]` block, which uses it anyway. The fault exists only in the translation
nobody runs here.

THE FORM THAT AVOIDS IT: a `cfg!()` CONSTANT instead of a `#[cfg]` attribute.

    const LAUNCHD_LIVES_HERE: bool = cfg!(target_os = "macos");
    ...
    None => LAUNCHD_LIVES_HERE.then(|| NOT_CHECKED.to_string()),

The function then exists once, compiles everywhere, references its callee everywhere, and folds to
the same code. `#[cfg]` stays right where the BODY needs an API that does NOT EXIST on the other
platform (`plist_path_for`, `RealCtl` — there it MUST be split); for a pure branch over the
platform it is the wrong tool.

A cross-check before pushing is not possible on this machine: `cargo clippy --target
x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` aborts on a C dependency ("failed to find tool x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc").
So CI really is the only gate here — consistent with [[gates-run-in-ci-not-locally]].

---

### `ci-cache-and-runtime-noise`

MEASURED 2026-09-04 over the logs of 32 `ci.yml` runs and the cache API, while fixing a repository
Actions cache that was evicting itself; sharpened afterwards in the review of that pull request.
Three things one otherwise gets wrong.

## 1. A SINGLE CI RUNTIME IS NOT A SIGNAL HERE

`Tests (debug)` in `quality-gates`, 30 successful runs in the same window:

    min 259 s   median 285 s   max 744 s   factor 2.9

and ALL THIRTY had a full cache hit. So the spread is NOT the cache; it is runner noise on shared
`ubuntu-latest` machines. Comparing two runs and deriving a decision from them is comparing noise.
This matters because this project decides an unusual amount on measured runtimes (dropping nextest
over 17 s, the macOS arrangement, the rule that CI is the gate). Anyone deciding such a thing anew
needs SEVERAL runs and the median, not one run.

## 2. THE CACHE HIT RATE IS HIGH — DO NOT TOUCH save-if

209 hits, 1 miss, every hit "full match: true" (so no re-saving). Anyone wanting to shrink the
Actions cache must NOT put `save-if:` or `cache-targets: false` on the CI lanes: there is no hit
rate to repair, and it costs. Measured, `changelog-check` would go from 40 s to 93 s per subsequent
run.

This count is kept CANONICALLY in the header comment of `.github/workflows/cache-sweep.yml`. It
stands here as well because a memory has to stand on its own — at session start that file is not
open. Whoever re-measures changes BOTH places.

The space comes from the sweeper instead: `.github/workflows/cache-sweep.yml` runs every six hours
and deletes what NO future run can read any more. The rule lives as a pure, unit-tested function in
`cargo xtask cache sweep` (`xtask/src/cache.rs`), not in the YAML. It depends solely on an entry's
`ref`: a deleted branch, the merge ref of a closed PR, a superseded release tag. `refs/heads/main`
and the newest tag always stay.

Effect on the first run: 32 entries / 10.67 GB -> 15 entries / 5.17 GB, against a hard limit of
10 GB per repository.

IF OCCUPANCY CLIMBS AGAIN, the first question is NOT "save less" but whether the sweeper is running
(`gh run list --workflow=cache-sweep.yml`).

And the second question needs a precision the review forced: the sweeper does NOT fall back to KEEP
throughout. Unknown ref shapes, an unreadable PR number and a missing newest tag — yes, those stay.
But the BRANCH arm DELETES ON ABSENCE: it removes `refs/heads/<b>` because `<b>` is not in the
branch list, and absence has two causes ("gone" and "not delivered"). That is why the list comes
from `git ls-remote --heads` (an unpaginated ref advertisement in which no page can be missing and
no namespace can hide) and NOT from `gh api .../branches`. Reverting that source turns it into a
deletion rule with an unknown basis.

Likewise a bet and not a guarantee: "the newest release tag stays, older ones do not". A tag is not
deleted when it is superseded, so it stays checkoutable; a re-run of an old release is possible,
just unlikely. Taken deliberately, because being wrong costs one cold rebuild — but it is not a
reachability fact like the other arms.

## 3. `actions/cache/usage` LIES IN THE SHORT TERM

The aggregate endpoint is eventually consistent. After a run that had demonstrably deleted 17 of 32
entries, it kept answering "32 entries, 10.67 GB" for FOUR MINUTES; the entry list `actions/caches`
said 15 / 5.17 GB immediately, and the aggregate only agreed from the sixth minute. To prove a
deletion, sum the LIST, not the aggregate — otherwise you quote exactly the number that proves
nothing happened.

### `call-graph-gate-joins-on-bare-names`

The write-seam gate in `crates/chat/tests/read_surface.rs`
(`nothing_on_this_seam_starts_work_that_was_not_already_commissioned`) does NOT decide by types or
modules which calls can start a session. It builds a call graph over ALL of `chat/src` and joins
nodes by **BARE FUNCTION NAME** (`nxs_test_support::verb_seam::call_graph` records every
`ExprMethodCall` and every `ExprCall` under its LAST path segment). For this gate two functions
with the same name are ONE function — `Workspace::resolve` and a private `WorkingCopy::resolve`
are the same node, and `tx.send(buf)` on an mpsc channel is the same node as `facade::send`.

THE CONSEQUENCE, measured 2026-09-05 while building the escalation-parking feature: a private
helper `fn resolve(&self, rev: &str)` in `crates/chat/src/park.rs`, in a module that shells out to
git via `std::process::Command` and whose pipe readers return their result through `tx.send(...)`,
turned ELEVEN READ VERBS of the engine seam red — `status`, `directory`, `search`, `thread`,
`prime_as`, `persona_prime`, `open`, `open_with`, `origin`, `definitions`, `withdraw`. The path the
gate found:

    status -> open -> resolve -> git -> send -> send_to -> channel_open -> ... -> trigger_and_bind

Every hop is real IN THE GRAPH and none is real in the code. The gate's error message names only
the eleven lines and says "the source is the one that is true" — it does NOT name the PATH, and
without it you look in the wrong place.

THE RULE THAT FOLLOWS: a private helper in `chat/src` must not share a name with something the
read seam calls — above all not `resolve`, `send`, `open`, `status`, `thread`, `search`,
`definitions`, `origin`. If you work in a module that spawns a subprocess or uses a channel, name
specifically: `resolve_commit`, not `resolve`. This is not cosmetics; it is the condition under
which this gate can say anything at all.

HOW TO FIND THE PATH when it happens anyway: a throwaway test in `crates/chat/tests/` that runs
`call_graph` over `crates/chat/src`, reverses the edges (callee -> caller) and runs a BFS backwards
from `trigger_and_bind` with a predecessor table; then print the path to the reported verb. Two
minutes, and delete it again afterwards.

### `golden-json-determinism-and-fixed-ids`

The golden-docs harness rests on two determinism properties, and both are easy to break from far
away.

1. KEY ORDER. `nxf` JSON determinism depends on `serde_json` NOT having the `preserve_order`
   feature: the default `BTreeMap` sorts keys lexicographically, which is the documented contract
   in `output.rs`. `xtask` must NOT enable `serde_json/preserve_order`. It would be a no-op for
   xtask's own struct-based artifacts (`commands.json` and the release-notes feed serialise in
   declaration order anyway) — but cargo FEATURE UNIFICATION leaks it into the `nxf` binary under
   `cargo test --all`, flipping `nxf`'s `Value` key order to insertion order and breaking the
   golden trycmd snapshots.

2. IDENTITY AND IDS. The env var `NXF_DETERMINISTIC_IDS` makes `nxf init` take a fixed identity
   (prefix `ab12`, site_id 1) and makes `create` mint sequential ids (`ab12.0001`…) via
   `ReplicaIds::mint_sequential`. Note that op_ids stay random ULIDs — that is CRDT identity and is
   never seeded — so golden lines carrying one are redacted with trycmd's `[..]` wildcard. The wall
   clock is pinned separately with `NXF_NOW`, because `close`/`archive` stamp their timestamps from
   `now`.

See [[golden-harness-runs-in-crate-dir]] for where the harness runs and what else it pins.

### `macos-ci-jobs-are-two-different-machines`

`macOS tests (hosted)` in ci.yml is the GitHub-HOSTED `macos-latest` runner (three cores), NOT the
org's own Mac. The self-hosted one is `Platform gates (macos)` (routed through the repository
variable `NXF_MACOS_RUNS_ON`, today `["self-hosted","macOS","ARM64"]`), and it runs `cargo clippy`
only — no tests at all.

WHY THIS MATTERS WHEN A RUN GOES RED. The two jobs fail for entirely different reasons and only one
of them can be reproduced by running cargo on the owner's machine:

- `macOS tests (hosted)`: three cores, shared, slow, and it runs
  `cargo test --no-fail-fast -p nxs -p nexus-chat -p nxs-service`. A test with a latent timing
  assumption fails HERE and nowhere else — 20 repeats on the owner's 10-core machine prove nothing
  about it. First measured case: nxf 6j6v.1zs2, where one tree answered PASS/FAIL/FAIL/PASS across
  four runs of this job.
- `Platform gates (macos)`: the org's own Mac, `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'`, clippy over
  the `#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]` code. A red here is a lint or a compile error, never a race.

CONSEQUENCE: when the hosted job reds on a test the diff does not touch, the first question is not
"what did I break" but "what is the failure RATE" — rerun that one job (`gh run rerun <id> --failed`)
before either accepting or blaming it, and compare against the same job's history on main
(`gh run view <id> --json jobs`). A single green run is what a 50% flake looks like half the time
([[gate-evidence-is-per-commit]]).

AND THE THING THAT IS NOT INNOCENT: adding tests to an existing test BINARY changes which tests run
beside each other on a three-core machine. A change that touches none of the failing code can still
raise a latent race's rate from never to often, and the honest way to say that is a hypothesis with
the run history beside it — not "not my change" and not a fix applied on a guess.

## A VERDICT CAN ALSO BE WRONG ABOUT ITSELF — read the rollup, not the check list

Absorbed here on 2026-09-18 from `ci-dispatch-cancels-the-open-prs-run`, a memory whose own body
recorded that its key named the direction the configuration does NOT support. What is real:

`git push` a new branch, `gh pr create` seconds later, and the arriving PULL_REQUEST run cancels the
in-flight PUSH run (measured 2026-09-11, PR #461). There `gh pr checks` shows every job PASSING — it
reports the surviving run — while `gh pr view --json mergeStateStatus` reads UNSTABLE and the merge
looks unsafe. The cancelled entry is visible ONLY in the rollup:

    gh pr view <n> --json statusCheckRollup --jq '.statusCheckRollup[]
      | select((.conclusion // .state) != "SUCCESS")'

A cancelled run whose successor SUCCEEDED seconds later is benign — compare `completedAt` of the
cancelled one with `startedAt` of the good one. UNSTABLE with every check green is that, and not a
reason to hold a merge.

And when a check reads `fail`, ask the API for the job's real conclusion before believing it:
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/jobs/<id> -q .conclusion` tells `cancelled` from `failure`,
which the PR check list does not. That is what a 2026-09-10 observation on PR #458 turned out to be
— a `managed-postgres` job reading `fail 35m1s` whose real conclusion was `cancelled`.

(Why a dispatch is safe beside an open PR, and why it is the only way to get macOS coverage on a
branch, is in [[gates-run-in-ci-not-locally]].)

### `macos-libressl-no-ed25519-blake2b`

SPIKE (2026-06-13): the macOS system `/usr/bin/openssl` is LibreSSL (3.3.6 tested) and supports
NEITHER `dgst -blake2b512` NOR Ed25519 ("Algorithm ed25519 not found", no ed25519 pkey algo). So
minisign-via-openssl verification CANNOT cover stock macOS — it works only where openssl is real
OpenSSL 1.1+/3.x (every Linux, and macOS with a Homebrew openssl).

This is an ALGORITHM-AVAILABILITY gap in LibreSSL, NOT a key-format issue — re-creating the signing
key does not help.

`install.sh` therefore probes CAPABILITY by self-test (`ossl_can_verify`: a blake2b512 plus
Ed25519 `-rawin` sign/verify round trip), never by version. Stock macOS is consequently left with:
install minisign (`brew install minisign`), OR set `NXF_INSECURE=1` to bootstrap on the verified
sha256 alone with a loud warning. Either way the UNCONDITIONAL gate is `nxs self-update`, which
always verifies minisign fail-closed and which every install can run afterwards.

An out-of-band public key (defence against an origin/CDN compromise) is a separate concern and not
solved by this. The strongest macOS first-install hardening is Developer-ID notarization (the Apple
membership is active) plus a Homebrew cask — notarization is the channel-independent trust anchor,
Homebrew is the channel.

### `oidc-no-repository-owner-condition`

GitHub OIDC role trusts in the shared nxsflow AWS accounts must **NOT** include a
`repository_owner` `StringEquals` condition — it breaks `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` with "Not
authorized" even when `aud`, `sub` and every other claim match. Proven 2026-06-11: every working
role omits it; only the two roles that carried it failed. Pin via the `sub` allow-list alone
(`repo:nxsflow/<repo>:…`), which already constrains the owner.

WHERE THE FIX LIVES NOW: it was originally made in this repo's `infra/lib/github-oidc.ts`. That
whole tree was deleted when the delivery stack moved into the nxsflowcom accounts on 2026-08-23;
the OIDC and deploy stacks now live in the `nxsflow-landing-page` repository. **The rule is
unchanged and still applies to every role in those accounts** — including the ones this repo still
assumes: `nxs-<env>-release` and `nxs-<env>-content-publish`. Only the file pointer moved.

WHAT THIS REPO STILL OWNS is the RELEASE, not the delivery: `release.yml`, `promote.yml`,
`publish-content.yml` and the two publish/promote scripts. They address the other side purely by
convention — role `nxs-<env>-release`, bucket `nxs-<env>-artifacts-<account>`, both built at
RUNTIME from the secrets `NXS_STAGING_ACCOUNT_ID` / `NXS_PROD_ACCOUNT_ID`. That is exactly why the
change of accounts reached them without a single line of edit, and why they survived the teardown
untouched.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT GITHUB FACT worth knowing: `workflow_dispatch`, tag, `workflow_run` and
`pull_request`-closed workflows only become triggerable once the workflow file is on the DEFAULT
branch (`main`) — so verify deploy/release workflows post-merge, via a dispatch. Its mirror image
holds too: DELETING such a workflow only stops it once the deletion is on `main`, so a teardown's
proof ("no run of it appears any more") is a post-merge observation, never a pre-merge one.

### `changelog-check-needs-a-commit`

`cargo xtask changelog check origin/main` detects fragments via `git diff --name-only
{base}...HEAD` (three-dot, i.e. merge-base) — see `xtask/src/changelog.rs::git_changed_paths`. On a
fresh feature branch with **no commits yet**, `origin/main...HEAD` is empty, so a correctly formed
`changes/<slug>.md` in the working tree — even staged — reports "this PR touches no changes/*.md
fragment". This is not a fragment-format problem: you simply have to make the commit first, and
then the check goes green.

It matters on every PR here because the `changelog-check` CI gate is fail-closed. It is also the
reason a green `changelog check` can be TRUE AND WORTHLESS if it ran before the fragment was
committed — see [[gate-evidence-is-per-commit]].

### `release-ring-policy`

OWNER DECISION 2026-08-02 — RELEASE RING POLICY: several consecutive BETA releases are explicitly
fine and are NOT a backlog.

The final proof of an idea ALWAYS happens in the apps — not in tests, not in the CLI. Only once an
idea has proven itself there and is meant to be published is the WHOLE CHAIN pulled to stable:
nexus-flow first, then app-foundations, then the affected app. That makes a promotion expensive;
that cost is accepted deliberately.

The owner will not be pushed into premature stable versions while something has only proven itself
in tests and a little in the CLI.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS REPO: a release may sit in the beta ring with a clear conscience, even when
unpromoted beta versions already sit in front of it. A release recommendation must NOT present that
as a problem. nexus-flow is the FIRST link in the chain when a promotion does happen.

---

### `release-cut-runbook`

CUTTING A RELEASE, end to end (`docs/specs/release-management.md` §10). Verified against the
workflows and xtask on 2026-09-18.

    cargo xtask version set <v>    # bump + fold changes/*.md into release-notes.json + regen docs
    # commit `chore(release): v<v>`, PR to main, ADD the skip-changelog LABEL, merge
    # WAIT for ci.yml to go green on the MERGE COMMIT, then:
    git tag -a v<v> -m "v<v>" && git push origin v<v>

`version set` is a chain in `xtask/src/main.rs`, not one function: validate fragments ->
enforce the major-bump migration -> enforce the facade-breaking axis -> bump Cargo.toml + lock ->
`changelog::consume` (folds the fragments into `release-notes.json` and DELETES them) ->
`docs::gen`.

WHICH AXIS: a pending fragment carrying `facade: breaking` forces a MINOR.
`enforce_facade_breaking_axis` fail-closes a PATCH bump carrying one, because by the §4.3 contract
a break ships only on the minor axis. Check `changes/*.md` for the marker before choosing the
number.

THE LABEL, AND WHY ITS TIMING COSTS TIME. A release PR DELETES fragments instead of adding one, and
the gate's diff is `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=ACMR {base}...HEAD`
(`xtask/src/changelog.rs::git_changed_paths`) — `ACMR` excludes Deletions, so the PR "touches no
fragment" and `changelog-check` is red BY CONSTRUCTION. Every release PR therefore carries
`skip-changelog`; set it right after `gh pr create`, before the check finishes. Adding it AFTERWARDS
does not fix the run, and RE-RUNNING does not either — a re-run replays the state the run started
with. The label has to be TOGGLED (remove, re-add). That cost the v0.92.0 session about ten minutes.

DO NOT PLAN A SECOND `docs gen`. `version set` regenerates `docs/generated` CORRECTLY, the man
page's version stamp included. This entry said the opposite until 2026-08-31, when v0.77.0 was cut
and the grep showed the new version already in both places; the old advice had been verified back at
0.2.1 and the tool had changed since. The second run is idempotent but costs a full xtask rebuild.
`cargo xtask docs check` afterwards is the evidence you actually need, and it is cheap.

THE WAIT BEFORE THE TAG IS NOT POLITENESS. Since 6j6v.31rs `release.yml` no longer runs the suite a
second time: `.github/scripts/require-green-ci.sh` READS the verdict of the `ci.yml` run for that
exact commit, counting only `push` and `workflow_dispatch` events, and is fail-closed — no green run
for the commit, red release, never a fallback test run. Merging to main produces exactly such a
`push` run, so no dispatch is needed there.

PROMOTION TO STABLE IS A MANUAL OWNER STEP: open the GitHub release, deselect "Set as pre-release",
set "Set as latest". That fires `promote.yml` (`release: types: [released]`), which SERVER-SIDE
COPIES the same bytes and signatures to stable — nothing is rebuilt or re-signed.

AND IF PROMOTE EVER COMPLAINS "no beta entry for <v> to promote": do NOT flip the GitHub release
first. Add the entry, re-run `version set`, then fire the promotion. That failure is now structurally
prevented — `consume()` ALWAYS writes the beta entry, upserting an empty `items: []` one when there
are no fragments, so "every released version is in the feed" holds from `version set` time, and
`assert_beta_entry()` (read-only, wired into promote.yml as `changelog assert-beta`) refuses early
instead of half-way. It is recorded because the half-promoted state it produced was expensive: on
v0.23.1 the operator had already flipped the release to stable when the first AWS step was skipped,
so GitHub said stable while S3 stable was empty.

A release with no user impact (a re-ship, a pure infra/CI patch) is a legitimate case and needs no
faked fragment.

A NEIGHBOURING TRAP ON THE SAME SURFACE, worth reading before the first push:
[[changelog-check-needs-a-commit]] — the check needs a COMMIT, so a correct fragment sitting in the
working tree reports as missing.

(Absorbed on 2026-09-18: `release-pr-skip-changelog`, `release-no-fragment-promote` and
`release-version-set-docs-gotcha`, which each carried one paragraph of the above and cost three
more lines of the session-start index than the facts needed.)
